提供跨学科对应：模型学习在自适应控制中称为"系统辨识"（system identification）；并指明其作为 Dyna 和 Adaptive RTDP 等间接强化学习方法的基础。

processed.definition: 间接强化学习是一种基于环境模型的强化学习方法，其经验通过模型间接地改进价值函数和策略，而非直接作用于二者。它是与直接强化学习相对的、由规划中介的方法，常被用来以更少的环境交互从有限经验中获得更好的策略。

supporting_observations.support: 原文明确指出 'experience can improve value functions and policies either directly or indirectly via the model'，并将 'indirectly via the model' 称为 indirect reinforcement learning，且 'is involved in planning'，直接锚定其基于模型、由规划中介的核心特征；同时给出与直接强化学习的对照以及'以更少环境交互从有限经验中获得更好策略'的性质描述。

processed.definition: search control 是 Dyna 架构中的一项过程，指选择模拟经验起始状态-动作对的机制，决定规划阶段从哪些已经历的状态-动作对中采样以产生由模型生成的模拟经验。它与模型学习、直接强化学习等组件并列，共同构成 Dyna 中模型-based 的一侧。

supporting_observations.support: 原文模型引用句直接定义 search control 为"选择模型生成的模拟经验起始状态和动作的过程"，并将其与 model learning、direct RL 并列于 Dyna 整体架构的模型-based 侧，完整锚定了该术语在 Dyna 框架内的角色与功能。

processed.definition: Dyna-Q is a tabular reinforcement learning algorithm that instantiates the Dyna architecture by tightly coupling one-step Q-learning, deterministic table-based model-learning, and planning: each real environment transition both updates the Q-function via one-step tabular Q-learning and records its outcome in a deterministic table model, after which the model is queried to produce n simulated transitions on which the same one-step Q-learning update is applied. Because learning and planning in Dyna-Q use exactly the same update rule—differing only in whether the transition is real or model-generated—the framework readily accommodates alternative value-update types or function approximators.

supporting_observations.support: Provides the canonical Dyna-Q description from Sutton & Barto §8.2: the pseudocode shows step (d) one-step tabular Q-learning on real experience, step (e) a deterministic table-model update, and step (f) n planning iterations that apply the same one-step Q-learning rule to model-generated transitions; the passage also states explicitly that 'learning and planning are accomplished by exactly the same algorithm, operating on real experience for learning and on simulated experience for planning.'

Refers to the Dyna-Q agent used in the blocking and shortcut maze experiments as the same §8.2 algorithm, confirming that Dyna-Q is treated as a complete integrated planning+RL agent (not a subroutine) and giving concrete experimental behavior consistent with the tabular architecture.

States that 'the Dyna-Q agents discussed earlier use q* sample updates, but they could just as well use q* expected updates, or either expected or sample qπ updates,' situating Dyna-Q within the update-type taxonomy and confirming that its shared update rule can be swapped—consistent with the definition that learning and planning differ only in the source of experience.

Describes the Dyna-Q agent as one that 'sample[s] uniformly ... from the state or state–action space,' anchoring the concrete planning-loop behavior (a random previously observed state–action pair queried in the model) shown in the §8.2 pseudocode and observation 1159.

References a 'neural net Dyna-Q system' (Miller & Williams, 1992), indicating that Dyna-Q is best understood as a Dyna-framework instantiation whose tabular model and Q-table can be replaced by neural function approximators, which the definition explicitly acknowledges.

processed.definition: Direct reinforcement learning is the component of the Dyna architecture in which the agent updates its value function directly from real experience obtained by interacting with the environment, in contrast to indirect (planning) methods that improve the value function using simulated experience from a learned model. In the Tabular Dyna-Q algorithm it is implemented by pseudocode step (d), which applies the one-step tabular Q-learning update to each observed transition, so that a nonplanning (n = 0) agent is equivalent to using direct reinforcement learning alone.

supporting_observations.support: Identifies direct reinforcement learning as one of three coordinated components of Dyna-Q — direct RL (step d), model-learning (step e), and planning (step f) — anchoring its identity as a distinct part of the Dyna architecture.

States that omitting steps (e) and (f) leaves one-step tabular Q-learning, directly supporting that direct reinforcement learning is realized as the one-step tabular Q-learning update applied to real experience.
Describes the n = 0 agent as a nonplanning agent that uses only direct reinforcement learning, supporting the claim that direct RL alone corresponds to a model-free one-step Q-learning agent.

processed.definition: Dyna-Q+ is a variant of the Dyna-Q reinforcement learning algorithm that promotes continual exploration by tracking, for each state–action pair, the number of time steps τ elapsed since that pair was last tried in a real interaction and adding a bonus reward κ√τ to the modeled reward during simulated planning updates. Compared with the base Dyna-Q agent, it additionally allows actions that have never been tried in a given state to participate in the planning step and initializes their model as a self-loop back to the same state with zero reward.

supporting_observations.support: Anchors the core identity of Dyna-Q+ as an enhanced Dyna-Q agent for continual exploration; provides the exact formula r + κ√τ, the role of τ as elapsed time steps since the pair was last tried, and the motivating scenario (blocking task, shortcut maze, changing environment dynamics) in which the algorithm was introduced.

Documents the two further modifications that distinguish Dyna-Q+ from plain Dyna-Q: allowing never-tried actions in the planning step and setting their initial model to a self-loop with reward zero. Both are explicitly attributed to 'the Dyna-Q+ agent', confirming they belong to the same algorithm's identity rather than to a separate method.

processed.definition: Optimistic modeling error is a type of model error in reinforcement learning in which the agent's learned model predicts greater rewards or better state transitions than the environment actually affords. Because planning produces policies that try to exploit these spurious opportunities, the agent quickly discovers through interaction that they do not exist, so the error tends to be detected and corrected relatively easily.

supporting_observations.support: The passage from Sutton & Barto's Chapter 8 defines the term as occurring 'when the model is optimistic in the sense of predicting greater reward or better state transitions than are actually possible,' and states that 'the planned policy attempts to exploit these opportunities and in doing so discovers that they do not exist,' directly anchoring the definition's claims about false opportunities, rapid discovery, and self-correction.

processed.definition: Computational curiosity is a planning heuristic in reinforcement learning that applies an exploration bonus to long-untried simulated transitions, encouraging the agent to keep testing all accessible state transitions and even to discover long action sequences. Realized in methods such as Dyna-Q+ and illustrated by the shortcut maze, the extra exploration it demands is often well worth its computational cost.

supporting_observations.support: The passage directly names 'computational curiosity' and characterizes it as the kind of testing that 'is well worth the extra exploration' in the shortcut maze, while the surrounding context links it to Dyna-Q+ and its exploration bonus on simulated transitions; this anchors both the heuristic nature of the concept and its concrete Dyna-Q+ implementation and shortcut-maze illustration.

processed.definition: An exploration bonus is a heuristic reward augmentation added to simulated planning experiences in the Dyna-Q+ algorithm, designed to encourage an agent to test state–action pairs that have not been tried for a long time and whose environment dynamics may have changed. Concretely, a modeled transition with reward r that has not been tried in τ time steps is treated in planning as if it produced reward r + κ√τ, for a small constant κ.

supporting_observations.support: Source passages from Section 8.3 describe the mechanism precisely: a 'special bonus reward' given on simulated experiences involving long-untried actions in Dyna-Q+, with the explicit formula r + κ√τ, used to encourage testing of state–action pairs whose dynamics may have changed. This directly anchors the definition's purpose, scope (planning/simulated experiences), and the specific reward-shaping formula.

processed.definition: 在强化学习中，stochastic environment 指状态转移和奖励由概率分布而非确定性函数刻画的环境。由于只能从其中观测有限数量的样本，据此学到的经验模型往往不够准确，因此环境本身的随机性常被视为模型误差（model error）的来源之一。

supporting_observations.support: P000922 中原文 'the environment is stochastic and only a limited number of samples have been observed' 直接支撑了'有限样本导致所学模型不准确'这一事实，同时 'environment is stochastic' 锚定了'环境动态具有随机性'这一核心义项；该段还指出随机性、函数近似泛化不完美、环境变化是模型错误的并列成因，说明随机环境被明确识别为一类独立的环境类型。

processed.entity: Prioritized Sweeping（强化学习规划算法）
processed.definition: 它是一种强化学习中的状态空间规划算法，通过维护一个按价值变化幅度排序的状态-动作对优先队列，将更新聚焦于价值真正发生变化的前驱，从而将变化沿状态空间高效地向后传播直至达到静止（quiescence）。该方法由 Moore 和 Atkeson（1993）与 Peng 和 Williams（1993）独立提出，对随机性问题使用期望更新，在迷宫等任务中相比无优先级的 Dyna-Q 通常可将求解速度提高数倍。

supporting_observations.support: 完整锚定核心机制：按价值变化幅度排序的优先队列、对前驱状态-动作对的反向更新、以小阈值为触发条件、以及"直到静止（quiescence）"的传播终止条件；同段还支持迷宫任务中比无优先级 Dyna-Q 快 5–10 倍的具体事实。
给出对算法搜索焦点的权威概括——"反向聚焦于最近价值发生变化的状态的前驱"，与上条共同支撑 definition 中反向传播与前驱定位的表述。
直接支持 definition 中关于提出者（Moore and Atkeson, 1993；Peng and Williams, 1993）及其后继工作（McMahan and Gordon, 2005；van Seijen and Sutton, 2013）的历史事实。
原文明确陈述"对于随机性问题，prioritized sweeping 总是使用某种期望更新完成"，直接支撑 definition 中"对随机性问题使用期望更新"的限定。
用 14400 状态的杆体操纵例子说明该方法在确定性、大规模问题上能解决无优先级方法难以处理的问题；并补充 small backups 可在其基础上进一步提升效率，体现其作为规划基线方法的地位。

processed.definition: Dyna 架构是由 Sutton (1990) 提出的、将规划、动作、模型学习与直接强化学习整合在同一智能体中的强化学习框架；其核心特征是同时利用真实经验与基于环境模型生成的模拟经验来更新同一价值函数或策略，属于在后台进行规划（background planning）的典型方法。

supporting_observations.support: 教材脚注直接说明 Dyna 架构由 Sutton (1990) 提出，并明确其整合规划、动作、模型学习与直接强化学习的结构，以及后续向线性函数逼近扩展的工作。
描述了 Dyna agents 把规划、动作、模型学习与直接强化学习整合在同一架构中，并指明基本形式下模拟转移从所有已历状态-动作对均匀随机地选起点，支持定义中'整合智能体框架'的表述。
'Dyna methods use both real and simulated experience to affect the same value function' 直接锚定其同时利用真实经验与模拟经验更新同一价值函数这一核心机制。
将 Dyna 与动态规划并列为后台规划（background planning）的典型代表，使用模型产生的模拟经验逐步改进策略或价值函数，支持定义中'后台规划典型方法'的定性。
Sutton (1991a) 论文标题 'Dyna, an integrated architecture for learning, planning, and reacting' 进一步从原作者角度确认 Dyna 作为整合学习、规划与反应三者的智能体架构的身份。

processed.definition: backward focusing 是强化学习状态空间规划中的一种更新排序策略：从价值发生变化的任意状态出发，沿前驱状态-动作对反向传播，仅对可能产生有用一步更新的动作执行更新，从而将规划计算聚焦于价值真正变化的位置。它与 forward focusing（按从频繁访问状态出发的可达性进行聚焦）等策略相对，是 prioritized sweeping 等高效规划方法背后的核心总体思想。

supporting_observations.support: 原文明确把 backward focusing 定义为从价值发生变化的任意状态反向沿前驱状态-动作对工作、仅做有用一步更新的'总体思想'（general idea），并强调不局限于 goal state，锚定了 definition 中关于反向传播机制和聚焦价值变化位置的核心内容。
原文指出本章所强调的 backward focusing 是一种 update ordering 策略，且明确把它与 forward focusing 并列对照（'backward focusing, but this is just one strategy'），支持 definition 中'更新排序策略'和与 forward focusing 相对的第二句解释。

processed.entity: quiescence（prioritized sweeping 中的静止终止状态）
processed.definition: 它是 prioritized sweeping 算法中的一个终止条件，指价值变化沿反向传播过程达到的静止状态：此时优先队列中已不存在超过更新阈值的状态-动作对需要处理，传播停止。

supporting_observations.support: 原文 'effects of changes are efficiently propagated backward until quiescence' 直接将 quiescence 锚定为 prioritized sweeping 中反向传播过程的终止点；观察标注的实体类型'终止条件'也支持该义项。

processed.definition: Peng and Williams (1993) 是 Peng 与 Williams 于 1993 年发表的一篇强化学习研究论文，在 Sutton 与 Barto《强化学习导论》第二版中被引为示例 8.4 中优先清扫（prioritized sweeping）在迷宫任务上较 Dyna-Q 取得 5 至 10 倍加速这一实验数据的来源。

supporting_observations.support: 源文本明确说明示例 8.4 中 prioritized sweeping 在迷宫任务上 'often by a factor of 5 to 10' 的加速数据 'Adapted from Peng and Williams (1993)'，同时给出实验设置（与图 8.2 同结构但网格分辨率不同的迷宫、每次环境交互最多 n=5 次更新），直接锚定该文献作为该实验结果的引用来源。

processed.definition: 在 prioritized sweeping 算法中，predecessor state–action pairs（又称 predecessor pairs）是指通过环境模型逆向回溯，被预测会转移到当前已被更新状态-动作对的状态-动作对；其估计价值的变化幅度越大，被赋予的更新优先级越高，越优先被插入更新队列。

supporting_observations.support: 原文明确将 predecessor pairs 定位为状态-动作对的一个子集（'predecessor pairs of those that have changed a lot'），并说明在 prioritized sweeping 中当队列顶部状态-动作对被更新时，会计算其对各 predecessor pairs 的影响（'the effect on each of its predecessor pairs is computed'），且按变化幅度排序入队（'prioritized by the size of the change'），从而锚定了'被预测转移到当前更新对的逆向回溯状态-动作对'以及'价值变化幅度越大优先级越高'这两条义项特征。

processed.definition: Moore and Atkeson (1993) 提出的强化学习规划基准任务：在有限矩形工作空间内将杆绕过障碍物以最少步数移至目标位置。它是确定性问题，有四个动作，杆可沿长轴或垂直方向平移或旋转，平移量约为工作空间的 1/20、旋转增量为 10 度，潜在状态约 14,400 个。

supporting_observations.support: 原始段落（P000948–P000949）直接给出任务目标（maneuver a rod around obstacles to a goal in fewest steps）、操作方式（沿长轴或垂直方向平移与旋转）、动作数（四个）、状态数（约 14,400）以及出处（Moore and Atkeson, 1993），完整锚定当前义项的事实细节。

processed.definition: Small backups 是一种用于强化学习规划的单步价值更新方法，由 van Seijen 与 Sutton (2013) 提出，它沿单条状态-动作转移执行更新，使用转移概率而非采样结果进行计算，因而兼具 expected update 的低方差与 sample update 的细粒度聚焦特性。通过精心选择 small backup 的执行顺序，其规划效率可大幅提升，超越 prioritized sweeping。

supporting_observations.support: 该 Observation 直接来自 Sutton & Barto 第 8.4 节，source_text 明确定义 small backups 为 'updates along a single transition, like a sample update, but based on the probability of the transition without sampling, as in an expected update'，并指出 'By selecting the order in which small updates are done it is possible to greatly improve planning efficiency beyond that possible with prioritized sweeping'，完整支撑了定义中关于单步更新、使用转移概率、兼具两种更新特性以及规划效率可超过 prioritized sweeping 的全部表述。

processed.definition: Forward focusing 是强化学习规划中的一种状态更新排序策略，按从当前策略频繁访问的状态出发到达某状态的难易程度来聚焦更新；它与 backward focusing 的传播方向互补，Peng and Williams (1993) 与 Barto, Bradtke and Singh (1995) 曾分别探索过其若干变体。

supporting_observations.support: 该 Observation 的 source_text 直接提供了 forward focusing 的核心定义（按从频繁访问状态出发到达目标状态的难易程度聚焦更新）、其与 backward focusing 的对应关系，以及 Peng and Williams (1993) 与 Barto, Bradtke and Singh (1995) 探索过其变体的事实，全部锚定当前义项。

processed.definition: q-policy evaluation is the one-step tabular algorithm that computes the action-value function q_π for a given policy by performing expected updates—sweeping over all possible next states, actions, and rewards at each backup. As the expected-update counterpart to sample-based methods such as Sarsa, it requires a distribution model of the environment and is one of the standard cases in tabular planning and learning.

supporting_observations.support: The passage from §8.5 ('Expected vs. Sample Updates') names the algorithm 'q-policy evaluation' and depicts it as a backup rooted at q_π(s,a) that fans out over all next states, actions, and rewards—i.e., an expected update—while the surrounding text explicitly contrasts expected updates with the sample updates used by methods like Sarsa. This directly anchors q-policy evaluation as the expected-update algorithm for the action-value function of a fixed policy.

processed.definition: q-value iteration is a dynamic programming / reinforcement learning algorithm that computes the optimal action-value function q* by repeatedly applying expected (full-backup) updates to action values. It is the action-value counterpart of value iteration and is typically contrasted with sample-based methods such as Q-learning.

supporting_observations.support: The observation identifies q-value iteration as a distinct one-step backup algorithm using expected updates of q*, and explicitly contrasts it with Q-learning in Figure 8.6 of Chapter 8, anchoring both the expected-update mechanism and the optimal action-value target.

processed.definition: Dyna-AC is a Dyna-style planning system in tabular reinforcement learning that integrates sampled planning with direct RL, distinguished from the related Dyna-Q by using v_π sample updates together with a learning policy structure rather than q* sample updates.

supporting_observations.support: The source text explicitly states 'The Dyna-AC system uses v_π sample updates' and locates it within the taxonomy of eight planning-update variants in Chapter 8, while contrasting it with Dyna-Q agents that 'use q* sample updates', thereby anchoring both the v_π sample-update target and its identity as a Dyna-family planning system.

processed.definition: 在强化学习中，分支因子（branching factor，记为 b）是指从给定状态-动作对出发可能到达的后继状态数，即满足估计的动力学 p̂(s'|s,a) > 0 的下一状态 s' 的个数。它由任务环境决定，直接决定了一次期望更新相对于一次采样更新所需的计算开销，并影响启发式搜索的可行深度。

supporting_observations.support: 给出分支因子的正式定义：b 为满足 p̂(s'|s,a) > 0 的可能后继状态数，并明确它决定期望更新与采样更新的相对计算量。
通过 b=2、b=10 等实验说明 b 的大小直接影响期望更新与采样更新在收敛效率上的差异，锚定定义中'决定计算开销'的论断。
在实验设置中明确'b 为任务的一个环境参数'，并对所有状态-动作对保持一致，支持定义中'由任务环境决定'的表述。
在 TD-Gammon 案例中给出有效分支因子约 400 的具体数值，说明该概念在博弈树搜索场景下同样适用，支持定义中'影响启发式搜索的可行深度'的补充。

processed.entity: sampling error（强化学习采样更新误差）
processed.definition: 在强化学习规划（planning）的语境中，采样误差是指采用 sample update（采样更新）时因仅依据单个采样得到的后继状态进行更新，而非对所有可能后继状态按概率求期望，所引入的额外随机误差；与之相对的 expected update（期望更新）对所有可能的后继状态做精确求和，因此不受该采样误差的污染。

supporting_observations.support: 原文明确指出 expected updates 'are uncorrupted by sampling error'，而 sample update 'is in addition a↵ected by sampling error'，并解释其原因是 'considers only one next state, not all possible next states'，直接锚定了该义项的核心内涵及其与期望更新的对比关系。

processed.definition: In reinforcement learning, a table-lookup representation stores the approximate value function as a table with one entry per state or state–action pair. It applies in the tabular case of discrete (finite) states and actions, where it can exactly represent any value function, and is typically contrasted with parametric function approximation when the state–action space becomes too large.

supporting_observations.support: Directly anchors the core definition: 'a table-lookup representation of the approximate value function, Q', explicitly situated in 'the special case of discrete states and actions', and used in the expected-update planning rule (Eq. 8.1).

Confirms that the table-lookup representation is the Part I (tabular) form in which 'any value function could be exactly approximated', and frames it in opposition to the parametric function approximation developed in Part II—supporting the contrast with function approximation in the definition.

Provides the converse constraint in the TD-Gammon case study: a lookup table cannot be used because the number of states is too large, which corroborates the definition's point that this representation scales only to finite state spaces and motivates switching to function approximation.

processed.definition: A reinforcement learning problem in which the environment is stochastic, such that, given a state and action, many possible next states may occur with various probabilities, so that the difference between expected and sample updates becomes significant (whereas with a single deterministic next state the two update types are identical).

supporting_observations.support: Observation 1218 directly states the canonical definition of a stochastic problem as one where the environment is stochastic and, given a state and action, many possible next states may occur with various probabilities; it also anchors the contextual fact that this stochasticity is what makes the difference between expected and sample updates significant, and that with only one next state the two update types are identical.

processed.definition: Trajectory sampling is a planning and update-distribution strategy in reinforcement learning that generates experience by simulating explicit individual trajectories under the current policy and performing updates at the states or state–action pairs visited along the way, rather than exhaustively sweeping the full state space. It is regarded as an efficient way of concentrating updates according to the on-policy distribution and is exemplified by algorithms such as RTDP, rollout methods, and trajectory-sampling search.

supporting_observations.support: Primary source defining the method in §8.6: 'one simulates explicit individual trajectories and performs updates at the state or state–action pairs encountered along the way. We call this way of generating experience and updates trajectory sampling,' and notes it is an efficient way of distributing updates according to the on-policy distribution.
Anchors the defining contrast with uniform state-space sweeps, describing trajectory sampling as updates 'focused on simulated on-policy trajectories, each starting in the same state.'

Provides the canonical algorithmic instance: RTDP is 'an on-policy trajectory-sampling version of the value-iteration algorithm,' and on-policy trajectory sampling 'allows the algorithm to completely skip states that cannot be reached by the given policy.'

Chapter-summary statement that trajectory sampling 'focuses on states or state–action pairs that the agent is likely to encounter when controlling its environment' and can 'skip over parts of the state space that are irrelevant to the prediction or control problem.'

Historical/contextual note: 'Trajectory sampling has implicitly been a part of reinforcement learning from the outset, but it was most explicitly emphasized by Barto, Bradtke, and Singh (1995) in their introduction of RTDP,' anchoring the concept's identity to that seminal reference.

processed.definition: 在强化学习中，on-policy distribution（常记作 µ 或 µ_π）是指执行当前（目标）策略 π 时，状态或状态-动作对上的访问概率分布；它在持续型任务中等同于 π 下的平稳分布，在回合制任务中等于按预期访问次数 η(s) 归一化后的结果。它是规划中按轨迹采样聚焦更新、加权平均价值误差（如 MSVE/VE）以及保证函数近似下半梯度方法收敛/稳定性的关键分布。

supporting_observations.support: 给出 on-policy distribution 的核心定义——'the distribution observed when following the current policy'，并直接说明其用于规划中按'轨迹采样'聚焦更新状态/状态-动作对，对照均匀/穷举扫描。
明确 µ(s) 即 'the fraction of time spent in s'，称为 on-policy distribution；在持续任务中等于 π 下的平稳分布，在回合制任务中由 η(s)/Ση(s′) 归一化得到（公式 9.3）。
复述核心定义 'the distribution of states encountered in an MDP while following the target policy'，并指出该概念可被推广为多个 on-policy distribution 的集合（依赖轨迹起始方式）。
指出 'Critical to these convergence results is that states are updated according to the on-policy distribution'，即该分布是 bootstrapping 与函数近似结合时保证半梯度方法收敛到 TD fixed point 的关键。
强调 'there are many on-policy distributions'——只要所有状态转移都来自目标策略，从不同起始方式（甚至含折扣作为部分终止）都能得到 on-policy distribution，且在任一这样的分布上训练线性半梯度方法都稳定。

processed.definition: 在强化学习规划中，将模型生成的更新通过对状态或状态–动作空间进行均匀采样来分布的一种更新分配策略，Dyna-Q 采用了该方式；与按 on-policy 分布等聚焦式采样相比，它因不把更新集中到最需要的部分而存在与穷举式扫描类似的问题。

supporting_observations.support: 原文明确指出均匀采样是 state/state–action 空间上的一种更新分配方式，由 Dyna-Q 使用，并因其不聚焦于最需要更新的位置而与穷举式扫描存在类似问题，为该义项的核心定义提供了直接锚定。
该段讨论了均匀分布更新与 on-policy 轨迹聚焦更新之间的相对效率对比，进一步支撑将均匀分布定位为 RL 规划中一种具体的更新分配策略，而非泛指概率论中的均匀分布。

processed.entity: 穷举式/均匀展开更新（强化学习规划）
processed.definition: 它是一种强化学习规划中的更新分配方式，不聚焦于特定轨迹，而是按状态空间均匀地展开更新；相较于 on-policy 轨迹采样这类聚焦方法，该方式至少在规模较小的问题上长期来看表现更优。

processed.definition: Real-time Dynamic Programming (RTDP) is an on-policy trajectory-sampling version of the value-iteration algorithm of dynamic programming, introduced by Barto, Bradtke, and Singh (1995), which updates the values of states visited along real or simulated trajectories by means of expected tabular value-iteration updates. As an asynchronous DP algorithm whose update order is dictated by the order states are visited in trajectories (generated by a greedy policy with respect to the current value function), it can focus computation on states relevant to the objective without performing exhaustive sweeps of the state set.

supporting_observations.support: Anchors the core definition: RTDP is an on-policy trajectory-sampling version of value iteration, uses expected tabular value-iteration updates on states visited in real or simulated trajectories, and is an asynchronous DP algorithm whose update order follows trajectory visitation.

Supports the greedy-policy and relevant-states emphasis: the trajectory-generating policy is always greedy with respect to the current value function, and RTDP focuses updates on fewer/relevant states rather than sweeping the full state set.

Supports the comparative framing in the definition: characterizes RTDP as an on-policy trajectory-sampling version of value iteration that illustrates advantages over conventional sweep-based policy iteration.

Supports the historical attribution to Barto, Bradtke, and Singh (1995), the relationship to Korf's LRTA* as an asynchronous DP algorithm generalized to stochastic problems, and the option of updating additional states between action executions.

processed.definition: The expected tabular value-iteration update is the one-step Bellman optimality backup for v* written in tabular form (equation 4.10 in Sutton & Barto), which replaces a state's value with the expectation of reward plus γ times the max-action value over next states. In RTDP it is applied to the states visited along an actual or simulated trajectory, and it may additionally be applied to any other collection of states such as those reached in a limited-horizon look-ahead search from the current state.

supporting_observations.support: P000981 explicitly identifies the operation as 'expected tabular value-iteration updates as defined by (4.10)' used by RTDP along trajectories; P000984 further specifies that RTDP 'applies the expected value-iteration update operation to the current state' and 'can also update the values of an arbitrary collection of other states at each step; for example, it can update the values of states visited in a limited-horizon look-ahead search from the current state,' which together anchor both the identity of the update and its two use cases in RTDP.

processed.definition: Relevant states are those that can be reached from at least one designated start state under some optimal policy, as opposed to irrelevant states that no optimal policy can reach from any start state. In a control problem this notion narrows the set of states on which an optimal policy must specify actions, and in practice it often comprises only a small fraction of all states reachable by arbitrary policies.

supporting_observations.support: Provides the canonical definition of relevant states (reachable from some start state under some optimal policy) and explicitly contrasts them with irrelevant states, anchoring the core meaning of the concept within a control-problem setting.

Reinforces the same definition and supplies the racetrack numerical example (9,115 states reachable by any policy, only 599 relevant), directly supporting the claim that relevant states are typically a small fraction of all states reachable by arbitrary policies.

processed.definition: In reinforcement learning, irrelevant states are states that cannot be reached from any start state under any optimal policy and therefore play no role in solving the prediction or control problem. An optimal partial policy may leave the actions at these states arbitrary or undefined, since they will never be encountered during execution.

supporting_observations.support: The passage from Sutton & Barto (2nd ed.), §8.7, explicitly labels 'Irrelevant States: unreachable from any start state under any optimal policy' and explains that such states are 'irrelevant to the prediction problem' and can be completely skipped, directly anchoring both the formal definition and the practical implication that their actions can be left unspecified.

processed.definition: In reinforcement learning, an optimal partial policy is a policy that specifies optimal actions only for the states deemed relevant to the task (e.g., those reachable under an optimal policy) while leaving actions for irrelevant states arbitrary or undefined. It relaxes the requirement of full optimality to a subset of states, and is motivated by planning settings such as Real-time Dynamic Programming (RTDP) where only some states need to be resolved.

supporting_observations.support: The passage explicitly defines an optimal partial policy as one that is optimal for the relevant states but can specify arbitrary actions, or even be undefined, for the irrelevant states, and situates the concept within RTDP and on-policy trajectory-sampling control to motivate why only a partial specification is needed.

processed.definition: A stochastic optimal path problem is a class of undiscounted episodic tasks for Markov decision processes with absorbing goal states that generate zero rewards, where the objective is to find a policy minimizing the expected cumulative cost of reaching a goal from any start state. It is traditionally formulated as cost minimization (rather than reward maximization), and includes prototypical examples such as minimum-time control tasks.

supporting_observations.support: Directly defines the entity as tasks satisfying the Barto–Bradtke–Singh conditions, explicitly states the cost-minimization framing, the equivalence between maximizing negative returns and minimizing path costs, and introduces minimum-time control as a representative example.

Identifies 'undiscounted episodic tasks for MDPs with absorbing goal states that generate zero rewards' as the underlying task setting from which stochastic optimal path problems arise, confirming the MDP context and the absorbing-goal/zero-reward structure of the problem class.

processed.definition: A class of stochastic optimal path problems in which each time step taken to reach a goal produces a reward of 1, so the objective is to reach the goal in the fewest time steps. Under the standard cost-minimization formulation it is equivalent to minimizing the number of steps along a path from a start state to a goal state.

supporting_observations.support: The passage explicitly names minimum-time control tasks as an example of stochastic optimal path problems and defines the reward scheme ('each time step required to reach a goal produces a reward of 1'), which directly anchors both the problem class and the fewest-steps objective in the definition; the surrounding sentence also links the reward-maximization view to cost-minimizing paths to a goal, supporting the equivalence clause.

processed.definition: Learning Real-Time A* (LRTA*) is a heuristic search algorithm introduced by Korf (1990) that is also characterized as an asynchronous dynamic programming method, originally developed for deterministic problems and applicable to stochastic problems as well. Its convergence properties were combined with Bertsekas's asynchronous DP results by Barto, Bradtke, and Singh (1995) to establish RTDP's convergence guarantee for stochastic optimal path problems.

supporting_observations.support: Anchors LRTA* as a 'heuristic search algorithm' due to Korf (1990) and records that Barto, Bradtke, and Singh (1995) combined its results with asynchronous DP results to prove RTDP's convergence for stochastic optimal path problems.

Anchors LRTA*'s characterization as 'an asynchronous DP algorithm' that applies to both stochastic problems and the deterministic problems Korf originally focused on, and specifies that Barto et al. (1995) combined Korf's LRTA* convergence proof with Bertsekas's asynchronous DP convergence result for stochastic shortest path problems.

processed.definition: The Racetrack problem is a stochastic optimal path problem in which an agent learns to drive a car around a turn and cross the finish line as quickly as possible while staying on the track, with a per-step reward of 1, start states at zero speed on the starting line, and episodes ending when the finish line is crossed (or the car is reset to a random start state if it hits the track boundary). As presented in Example 8.6 of Sutton & Barto, it imposes no speed limit and serves as a benchmark for comparing RTDP with conventional DP value iteration.

supporting_observations.support: Anchors the core definition: stochastic optimal path problem, car driving around a turn, crossing the finish line, start states as zero-speed states on the starting line, goal states reachable in one step from inside the track, per-step reward of 1, and boundary-hit reset to a random start state; also confirms the no-speed-limit version used in Example 8.6.

Supports the Example 8.6 usage as a benchmark comparing RTDP with conventional DP value iteration, and provides concrete state counts (9,115 reachable, 599 relevant) for the specific racetrack instance used; also confirms the evaluation metric (number of steps to cross the finish line).

processed.definition: An absorbing goal state in a Markov Decision Process (MDP) is a terminal goal state that, once reached, yields zero reward and self-loops indefinitely rather than transitioning elsewhere. It is a defining feature of undiscounted episodic tasks such as stochastic optimal path problems, where reaching it ends an episode and the RTDP convergence theorem additionally requires that all rewards for transitions from non-goal states be strictly negative.

supporting_observations.support: Directly anchors all components of the definition: the 'goal states... that generate zero rewards and absorb the trajectory' phrasing defines the core concept; the 'undiscounted episodic tasks for MDPs with absorbing goal states' clause places it within episodic MDPs; 'stochastic optimal path problems' identifies the typical problem class; and the RTDP conditions ('initial value of every goal state is zero' and 'all rewards for transitions from non-goal states are strictly negative') are stated as theorem-level requirements rather than as definitional properties of the state itself.

processed.definition: Cost minimization is an alternative optimization formulation for stochastic optimal path problems, in which the objective is to find a path from a start state to a goal state with the minimum accumulated cost. It is mathematically equivalent to the reward-maximization formulation used in reinforcement learning, because maximizing the negative of each step's reward corresponds to minimizing the total cost along the path.

supporting_observations.support: The source passage explicitly states that stochastic optimal path problems 'are usually stated in terms of cost minimization instead of as reward maximization' and that 'maximizing the negative returns in our version is equivalent to minimizing the costs of paths from a start state to a goal state,' directly anchoring both the identity as an alternative formulation and its equivalence to reward maximization.

processed.definition: Gauss-Seidel value iteration is a variant of value iteration that updates the value of one state at a time in place, with each update immediately using the most recently updated values of the other states rather than values from the previous sweep. Compared with the Jacobi version, which retains a separate copy of the value array between sweeps, this in-place scheme was observed to converge roughly twice as fast on the racetrack example in Sutton and Barto.

supporting_observations.support: The passage explicitly identifies the algorithm as 'the Gauss-Seidel version of value iteration,' defines its in-place single-state update rule ('the update for each state uses the most recent values of the other states'), and provides the empirical comparison ('approximately twice as fast as the Jacobi version on this problem') on the racetrack task.

processed.definition: Jacobi value iteration is a variant of value iteration in which state-value updates within each sweep rely on the value estimates from the previous sweep rather than on the most recent values updated earlier in the same sweep, and is typically contrasted with the Gauss-Seidel version of value iteration. In the racetrack example from Sutton and Barto's reinforcement learning textbook, the Gauss-Seidel version was reported to be approximately twice as fast as the Jacobi version.

supporting_observations.support: Identifies Jacobi value iteration as a version of value iteration (algorithm variant) and directly anchors the comparative performance fact: on the racetrack example the Gauss-Seidel version was found to be approximately twice as fast as the Jacobi version, with the passage situating this comparison in a discussion of exhaustive-sweep DP.

processed.definition: Background planning is a use of planning in reinforcement learning that gradually improves a policy or value function through simulated experience generated from a model, rather than concentrating computation on the current state. It is typified by dynamic programming and Dyna, and is contrasted with decision-time planning, which instead focuses on selecting an action for the current state.

supporting_observations.support: P000996 explicitly defines background planning as using planning to gradually improve a policy or value function on the basis of simulated experience from a model, states it is not focused on the current state, and names dynamic programming and Dyna as exemplars. P000997 completes the contrast with decision-time planning, which focuses on the current state, anchoring the key distinguishing feature in the definition.

processed.definition: Decision-time planning is a way of using a model in reinforcement learning in which planning begins and completes after the agent encounters each new state St, with its output being the selection of a single action At by evaluating many predicted state and reward trajectories emanating from the current state. It is distinguished from background planning by concentrating computation on the current state rather than on improving a global value function or policy, and the values and policy it produces are typically discarded once the current action is chosen.

supporting_observations.support: Provides the core definition directly from §8.8: planning begins and completes after each new state, outputs a single action, focuses on a particular state, may look deeper than one-step-ahead, evaluates many predicted state/reward trajectories, and the values and policy created are typically discarded. Also explicitly contrasts it with background planning.

Identifies heuristic search as the classical AI example of decision-time planning, and states that decision-time planning can produce better decisions than unfocused updates by concentrating on states/actions immediately downstream from the current state—reinforcing the focus-on-current-state characterization.

Characterizes planning at decision time as the most important form of forward-focused planning from pertinent (actually encountered) states during agent-environment interaction, and reiterates that classical heuristic search is an example.

Shows rollout algorithms as concrete decision-time planning algorithms that simulate trajectories from the current state, immediately use the resulting action-value estimates to select an action, and then discard them—directly instantiating the 'select then discard' property.

Cites MCTS as a striking real-world example of decision-time planning executed after each new state, and notes its applicability to games and single-agent sequential decision problems when a model allows fast multistep simulation.

processed.definition: An expected update with max is a tabular dynamic-programming backup operation that first takes an expectation over next states (and rewards) and then a maximization over actions, thereby computing the Bellman optimality backups for the optimal state-value function v* and the optimal action-value function q*. It is the same form of one-step backup used throughout the book whenever v* or q* are updated, and the value backup performed at the leaf nodes of a heuristic search tree reduces to exactly this operation before being propagated up to the current state.

supporting_observations.support: The passage explicitly identifies 'expected updates with maxes' as the backup operations for v* and q* and states that 'the backing up within the search tree is just the same as in the expected updates with maxes,' directly anchoring both the optimal-value-function target and the identity with heuristic-search backups.

processed.definition: A perfect model in reinforcement learning is a model of the environment that is without error, used as the planning component in model-based methods. A key theoretical consequence is that when a perfect model is paired with an imperfect action-value function, deeper search through the model will generally yield better policies, and if the search is carried all the way to the end of the episode, the effect of the imperfect value function is eliminated entirely.

supporting_observations.support: The passage directly defines a perfect model as a model of the environment that is perfect (without error) and states the core theoretical results: deeper search with a perfect model and imperfect action-value function yields better policies, and searching to the end of the episode eliminates the effect of the imperfect value function. The TD-Gammon example is given as an empirical illustration but is not part of the definition itself.

processed.definition: Self-play (reinforcement learning) 是一类强化学习训练范式，由学习系统（或其拷贝/早期版本）作为博弈双方互相对弈来生成训练经验，每局对局通常被视作一个 episode。 该范式在二人完备信息博弈中尤为典型，已被 TD-Gammon（用于学习 afterstate 价值函数）、AlphaGo 与 AlphaGo Zero（用于训练策略网络与价值网络）等系统采用，但在非完备信息或智能体行为与人类对手差异显著的场景（如 Watson 的 Jeopardy! 博弈）中可能不适用。

supporting_observations.support: 直接定义 self-play 为"a system plays against itself"的训练范式，并锚定 TD-Gammon 用 many games of self-play 学习 afterstate value function 的具体事实。
阐述 self-play 的具体实现机制：TD-Gammon 通过让学习程序与自身对弈生成"unending sequence of games"，每局作为一个 episode、序列位置作为状态 S0,S1,S2,...，并通过约 300,000 局自博弈达到与基于专家知识的程序相当的水平。
把 self-play 定位为跨多个里程碑系统的通用训练范式："All these programs included reinforcement learning over simulated games of self-play"，涵盖 Samuel 的西洋跳棋程序、TD-Gammon、AlphaGo 和 AlphaGo Zero，确立其作为通用范式而非单一系统特性。
锚定 AlphaGo Zero "learned exclusively from self-play reinforcement learning" 的具体事实，并指出其无需人类数据或指导，仅以棋盘落子"raw"描述作为输入，体现 self-play RL 的纯自学习性质。
通过反例刻画 self-play 的适用边界：Watson 的 Daily-Double 价值函数未采用自博弈，因为 Jeopardy! 是不完备信息博弈且 Watson 与人类对手差异显著，自博弈会探索到不典型的状态空间区域。

processed.definition: One-step updates are individual single-step backup operations in reinforcement learning planning, each propagating a value estimate across a single state transition. When performed in sequence from the leaves toward the root, a collection of these updates can implement heuristic search, and the empirical advantage of deeper search is attributed to concentrating computation on states and actions near the current state rather than to the use of multistep backups as such.

supporting_observations.support: The source text directly states that heuristic search can be constructed by performing 'individual, one-step updates from bottom up,' and that 'the performance improvement observed with deeper searches is not due to the use of multistep updates as such' but rather to focusing updates on states and actions immediately downstream from the current state—exactly the two key claims in the definition.

processed.definition: A search tree traversal strategy used in reinforcement learning planning in which nodes are explored in a selective depth-first order, thereby defining the sequence of one-step value updates applied during heuristic search. It concentrates computational effort on states and actions near the current state by backing up values from leaf nodes toward the root in this specific order, and yields the same overall update as depth-first heuristic search when combined with a tabular representation.

supporting_observations.support: The passage explicitly describes selective depth-first search as a traversal/ordering strategy for the one-step updates that implement heuristic search (Figure 8.9), and notes that with a tabular representation the same overall update is achieved as in depth-first heuristic search. The figure caption confirms the ordering of bottom-up backups as a selective depth-first search.

processed.definition: A search tree is a tree data structure used in decision-time planning whose root node represents the current state and whose branches expand to possible future states and actions (continuations). It is incrementally built or traversed by search algorithms—such as heuristic search or Monte Carlo Tree Search—to evaluate continuations and guide action selection, and is typically tightly focused on states and actions near the current state.

supporting_observations.support: Anchors the core concept of a search tree as a 'tree of possible continuations' from a state, with the value function applied at leaf nodes and values backed up to the root; establishes the heuristic-search context and the property that the tree is tightly focused on states and actions immediately following the current state.

Confirms the search tree as a tree data structure whose root represents the current environment state, incrementally extended and traversed by MCTS, with edges carrying statistics; also shows that across successive MCTS executions a portion of the tree (descendants of the new root) may be retained, supporting the general property that the tree is rebuilt or partially reused at each planning step.

processed.definition: Backed-up values are values computed at state–action nodes by propagating estimates backward from the leaf nodes of a search tree. In heuristic search and decision-time planning they are transient—used to choose the best action for the current state and then discarded, without being saved by updating the approximate value function.

supporting_observations.support: The primary source for this entity: explicitly states that backed-up values are computed by backing up from the leaf nodes to the state–action nodes of the current state, that they are not saved by changing the value function in conventional heuristic search, and that they are discarded once the best action is chosen.

Provides a concrete planning/search application (Samuel's checkers player) where the same notion of propagating scores backward from terminal positions through a search tree to the root is called a 'backed-up score', confirming the concept's identity as backward-propagated search-tree values rather than a procedure or data structure.

Uses the same term 'backed-up values' in a wider RL sense (e.g., full Monte Carlo return, n-step Sarsa returns) as update targets, indicating that the heuristic-search usage is one instance of the broader idea of values produced by backward propagation.

processed.definition: State–action nodes are nodes in a heuristic search tree that each represent a state–action pair, forming the level at which the value backup terminates when estimates are propagated from the leaf nodes back toward the current state; the action associated with the node carrying the best backed-up value is then selected as the current action.

supporting_observations.support: The passage directly states that heuristic search builds a tree of possible continuations from each state, that the value backup stops at the state–action nodes for the current state, and that the best of the resulting backed-up values is chosen as the current action—exactly the role captured in the definition.

processed.definition: Rollout Algorithms 是一类基于 Monte Carlo control 的决策时规划算法，在每个决策时刻从当前环境状态出发沿给定 rollout policy 模拟大量轨迹，通过对这些轨迹的回报取平均来估计当前状态下各动作的动作值，并据此选择并执行估值最高的动作。与标准 Monte Carlo control 不同，它们不学习或存储全局动作值函数，而是只对当前状态产生一次性估计、用后即弃，并在到达下一状态后重复该过程。

supporting_observations.support: 提供了权威定义原文：决策时规划算法、基于 Monte Carlo control、沿 rollout policy 模拟大量轨迹并对回报取平均、贪心选择估值最高动作、估计用后即弃、不估计完整 q* 或 qπ。
明确将 rollout algorithm 与 MCTS 区分：rollout algorithm 每次动作都运行大量完整回合的 Monte Carlo 模拟但不增量扩展搜索树，锚定了 '不存储全局/部分动作值函数、用后即弃' 的边界。
指出 MCTS 'at its base' 是 rollout algorithm，验证了决策时模拟多条轨迹至终止态并平均回报的核心机制，同时也说明 MCTS 是其增强形式而非等同物。
锚定历史与应用事实：Abramson (1990) 的 expected-outcome model、Tesauro & Galperin (1997) 在 backgammon 中的应用、'rollout' 一词的掷骰子来源、Bertsekas 等在组合优化中的使用。
章节总结中将其与 MCTS 并列为 'decision-time planning' 受益于在线、增量、基于样本的价值估计与策略改进的范例，支撑其上位类别为决策时规划算法。

processed.definition: Rollout policy（rollout 策略）是 rollout 算法和蒙特卡洛树搜索（MCTS）等决策时规划方法中，用于在模拟轨迹（rollout）里选择动作的基础策略，通常选取实现简单、计算开销低的策略以快速生成大量模拟样本。其作用是提供用于蒙特卡洛动作值估计的采样策略，算法的目标在于基于这些估计构造一个优于 rollout policy 本身的改进策略，而非寻找全局最优策略。

supporting_observations.support: 锚定 rollout policy 的核心身份：rollout 算法在模拟轨迹中遵循的给定策略 π；算法沿其模拟以估计各动作值；目标是改善该策略本身而非寻找最优策略（'the aim of a rollout algorithm is to improve upon the rollout policy; not to find an optimal policy'）。

Characterizes incremental, online settings as the most natural setting for the RL algorithms emphasized in the book, while noting that current deep learning methods struggle with this paradigm (catastrophic interference), confirming its identity as the RL-specific online learning requirement.

processed.definition: Semi-gradient TD(0) is a one-step temporal-difference algorithm for estimating a state-value function under function approximation, in which the update target bootstraps on the current value estimate, Ut = Rt+1 + v̂(St+1, w), but the dependence of that target on the weight vector is ignored when computing the update—hence the term "semi-gradient." It is the n=1 special case of n-step semi-gradient TD, runs fully online in continuing problems, and under linear function approximation converges (via a theorem beyond general SGD) to the TD fixed point w_TD = A⁻¹b with only O(d) per-step computation and memory.

supporting_observations.support: Establishes the canonical update target Ut = Rt+1 + v̂(St+1, w), labels semi-gradient TD(0) as the 'prototypical semi-gradient method', and notes that the update is continual and online, enabling use on continuing problems.

Identifies semi-gradient TD(0) as the n=1 special case of n-step semi-gradient TD and explains the defining 'semi-gradient' property: in bootstrapping the weight vector appears in the update target but is not accounted for in the gradient computation.

Provides the convergence characterization: under linear function approximation semi-gradient TD(0) converges, but this requires a theorem beyond general SGD, and the limit is the TD fixed point w_TD = A⁻¹b, which is near—not equal to—the global optimum of the value error.

Anchors the computational profile: semi-gradient TD(0) needs only O(d) memory and per-step computation, in contrast to the O(d²) cost of LSTD, helping identify it as a lightweight one-step linear TD method.

processed.definition: State aggregation is a simple form of function approximation in reinforcement learning in which states are grouped into disjoint aggregates, each sharing a single estimated value as one component of the weight vector w. It is a special case of both linear function approximation and stochastic gradient descent, is equivalent to using a single non-overlapping tiling, and sits on the function-approximation spectrum between tabular methods and richer representations such as coarse coding.

supporting_observations.support: Provides the canonical formal definition: states grouped together, one estimated value (one component of w) per group, and a special case of SGD (9.7) whose gradient is 1 for the group's component and 0 elsewhere.
States explicitly that 'state aggregation is a special case of linear function approximation', anchoring the linear-FA relationship in the definition.
Equates state aggregation with a single non-overlapping tiling (generalization complete within a tile, none across tiles) and contrasts it with coarse coding, which uses multiple overlapping tilings.

Places state aggregation on the function-approximation spectrum 'ranging from tabular methods at one extreme through state aggregation, a variety of linear methods, and then a diverse set of nonlinear methods', supporting its intermediate position.
Supplies historical anchoring: earliest RL use attributed to Michie and Chambers's BOXES system (1968), and prior use in dynamic programming from Bellman (1957a).

processed.definition: 随机梯度下降（SGD）是一类迭代优化方法，其在每个训练样本（或小批量）后沿该样本目标（如均方误差）负梯度的方向以小步长调整参数，使总体上以随机方式最小化平均性能度量。在强化学习中，它被用于值预测的函数逼近，其一般权重更新形式即方程 9.7（在线性函数逼近下梯度化简为特征向量 x(s)），状态聚合是该一般形式的一个特例。

supporting_observations.support: 给出 SGD 在值预测函数逼近中的核心定义：单样本更新、沿负梯度方向、适合在线强化学习；这是最权威的概念锚点。
明确将状态聚合刻画为 SGD（方程 9.7）的特例，并给出梯度的 0/1 形式，支持定义中'状态聚合是特例'的原文事实。
给出 SGD 的更新公式 9.7 及其在线性函数逼近下的简化形式，直接支持定义中关于方程 9.7 和线性化简的表述。
给出 SGD 的通用定义：更新在期望上等于目标函数负梯度、期望上沿目标下降、稳定性与收敛性优良，支撑定义首句的'迭代优化方法'通常含义。
明确'SGD 是寻找好权重向量最流行的方法'，支撑定义中关于其作为通用优化框架的稳定特征。

processed.definition: The 1000-state Random Walk is a specific Markov reward process benchmark task introduced in Sutton & Barto's reinforcement learning textbook, in which 1000 states are arranged in a line (numbered 1 to 1000), every episode begins near the center at state 500, and each step transitions with equal probability to one of up to 100 neighboring states on either side (with edge effects adding termination probability near the boundaries), yielding a terminal reward of +1 on the right and −1 on the left and 0 otherwise. It is used as a running example throughout Chapter 9 to illustrate and compare linear function approximation methods, including state aggregation, semi-gradient TD(0) versus gradient Monte Carlo, and feature constructions such as Fourier and polynomial bases.

supporting_observations.support: Provides the canonical specification of the task: 1000 states numbered 1–1000, episodes starting at state 500, transitions of up to 100 states left/right with equal probability, edge effects adding termination probability, and rewards of +1 (right), −1 (left), 0 otherwise; also states it is used as a running example throughout the section.

Confirms the same task is reused in Example 9.2 to illustrate linear function approximation (state aggregation as a special case) and to compare semi-gradient TD(0) with gradient Monte Carlo, including a 20-group re-aggregation matched to the 19-state tabular random walk.

Shows the task continuing as a benchmark in Section 9.5.2, where learning curves under gradient Monte Carlo are compared across Fourier and polynomial bases of orders 5, 10, and 20, reinforcing its role as a reusable illustration vehicle across the chapter.

processed.definition: Gradient Monte-Carlo algorithm is the gradient-descent form of approximate Monte Carlo state-value prediction, which uses the Monte Carlo return G_t as an unbiased target and updates the weights w of a differentiable value-function approximator v̂(s, w) under the standard stochastic gradient-descent rule w ← w + α[G_t − v̂(S_t, w)]∇v̂(S_t, w). Under linear function approximation and the usual step-size conditions it converges to the global optimum of the value error VE, and it corresponds to the n = ∞ special case of the n-step semi-gradient TD family.

supporting_observations.support: Anchors the core identity: 'gradient-descent version of Monte Carlo state-value prediction' that uses the Monte Carlo target G_t with the standard SGD update, and is guaranteed to find a locally optimal approximation to v_π. Provides the pseudocode and update formula.
Supports the convergence claim: under linear function approximation and the usual decreasing-step-size conditions, the algorithm converges to the global optimum of the VE.
Supports the 'n = ∞ special case of n-step semi-gradient TD' characterization, locating the algorithm within the broader semi-gradient TD family.
Provides the canonical 1000-state random walk demonstration with state aggregation (100,000 episodes, α = 2×10⁻⁵), where the learned values approach the global minimum of the VE.

Shows the same algorithm applied with Fourier and polynomial bases (orders 5, 10, 20) on the 1000-state random walk, confirming it is used as a general gradient-MC method independent of any single feature scheme.

processed.definition: It is a semi-gradient temporal-difference algorithm for policy evaluation under function approximation, whose key update (equation 9.15) steps in the direction of the gradient of the approximate value using the n-step return as the target. It is the function-approximation extension of the tabular n-step TD method, with semi-gradient TD(0) and gradient Monte Carlo recovered as its limiting special cases.

supporting_observations.support: Gives the defining update equation 9.15, w_{t+n} = w_{t+n-1} + α[G_{t:t+n} − v̂(S_t, w_{t+n-1})]∇v̂(S_t, w_{t+n-1}) for 0 ≤ t < T, which is the core identity of the n-step semi-gradient TD algorithm.

States that the algorithm is 'the natural extension of the tabular n-step TD algorithm presented in Chapter 7 to semi-gradient function approximation' and provides the full pseudocode, anchoring its role as the function-approximation counterpart of tabular n-step TD.

Identifies the algorithm as the natural policy-evaluation method under function approximation and states that it includes gradient Monte Carlo and semi-gradient TD(0) as its special cases, anchoring the limiting-case relationship in the definition.
References equations (9.15) and (9.16) as the definition of the two-step semi-gradient TD method, confirming that the n=2 case is an instance of the same algorithm family described here.

Discusses 'Linear semi-gradient n-step TD' as the same algorithm under linear function approximation, confirming that the general n-step semi-gradient TD identity carries over to specialized contexts.

processed.entity: 特征交互（机器学习/线性函数逼近）

processed.definition: Fourier series is a mathematical representation that expresses a periodic function as a weighted linear combination of sine and cosine basis functions whose frequencies are integer multiples of a fundamental frequency. It is a foundational tool in Fourier analysis, widely used in applied sciences to approximate functions to arbitrary accuracy, and can serve as a basis for linear function approximation methods.

supporting_observations.support: The passage directly defines the Fourier series as expressing periodic functions as weighted sums of sine and cosine basis functions of different frequencies, explains the one-dimensional representation with periods dividing τ (frequencies as integer multiples of 1/τ), and notes its broad use in applied sciences for approximating functions and as a basis for linear function approximation in reinforcement learning.

processed.definition: Fourier basis is a set of sine and cosine basis functions at different frequencies that express a function as a weighted linear combination, serving as one of the standard approaches to linear function approximation. In reinforcement learning, it is widely adopted for feature construction because, given enough terms, it can approximate periodic functions to arbitrary accuracy, though its features are global (non-zero across the state space) and the number of order-n features grows exponentially with the state-space dimension.

supporting_observations.support: Anchors the core identity: Fourier basis is a linear function approximation method based on the Fourier series, expressing periodic functions as weighted sums of sine and cosine basis functions of different frequencies, and establishes its use in RL feature construction.

Supports the accuracy claim (enough basis functions can approximate essentially any function), the exponential growth of order-n features with state-space dimension, the global (non-zero) nature of the features, and the comparison showing Fourier features outperforming or competing with polynomial and radial basis functions in RL.

Supports the claim that Fourier basis is preferred over polynomials in the online learning setting typical of RL, and anchors the attribution that it was introduced in a simple RL-suitable form by Konidaris, Osentoski, and Thomas (2011) for multi-dimensional continuous state spaces.

processed.definition: The Fourier transform is a mathematical integral transform that generalizes the Fourier series by decomposing a function into its constituent frequency components. It is widely used in applied sciences to approximate functions, expressing them as weighted combinations of sinusoidal basis functions whose coefficients can be computed by simple formulae.

supporting_observations.support: The source text explicitly identifies the Fourier transform as 'the more general' form beyond the Fourier series, states it is 'widely used in applied sciences' for function approximation, and notes that basis function weights are given by 'simple formulae' and that 'essentially any function can be approximated as accurately as desired' with enough basis functions.

processed.definition: A periodic function is a function whose values repeat at regular intervals, formally defined as a function f satisfying f(x) = f(x+τ) for all x and some period τ. Periodic functions are commonly expressed via Fourier series as weighted sums of sine and cosine basis functions of different frequencies.

supporting_observations.support: The passage directly states the formal definition 'A function f is periodic if f (x) = f (x + τ) for all x and some period τ' and establishes the characteristic property of value repetition over a period; it also supports the Fourier series connection by describing periodic functions as 'weighted sums of sine and cosine basis functions (features) of different frequencies.'

processed.definition: A basis function family composed solely of sine functions, used as an alternative to the cosine basis in Fourier-type feature construction for linear approximation methods. Its linear combinations are always odd (anti-symmetric about the origin) functions, paralleling how the cosine basis represents even functions over a half-period interval.

supporting_observations.support: Directly provides the canonical characterization: 'sine features, linear combinations of which are always odd functions, that is functions that are anti-symmetric about the origin'; the same passage contrasts the sine basis with the cosine basis within Fourier feature construction, supporting the second sentence of the definition.

processed.definition: A basis composed of cosine functions, typically expressed as features of the form x_i(s) = cos(iπs) in one dimension or x_i(s) = cos(π sᵀc_i) in higher dimensions, used for function approximation over a bounded interval. Because any linear combination of cosine features is an even function (symmetric about the origin), the cosine basis can represent any even function and is commonly used to approximate non-periodic functions by restricting attention to a half-period, where it is generally preferred over the sine basis.

supporting_observations.support: Anchors the core meaning: the cosine basis is formed by cosine features and can represent any even function (symmetric about the origin), which is the defining mathematical property used to justify its use over a half-period interval.

Provides the explicit one-dimensional form of the cosine basis: the order-n version with τ=2 over [0,1] consists of features x_i(s) = cos(iπs) for i = 0, …, n, with x_0 being a constant function. Also supplies the standard global alias 'Fourier cosine basis'.

Supports the claim that the cosine basis is used to approximate non-periodic functions over a bounded interval (the half-period), that it is the variant recommended over the sine basis, and supplies the multi-dimensional form x_i(s) = cos(π sᵀc_i) along with context about its use in RL feature construction.

Confirms the k-dimensional extension and the order-n truncation convention, showing that the cosine basis generalizes beyond the one-dimensional case and that the number of features grows as (n+1)^k with state-space dimension.

processed.definition: 偶函数是满足 f(x) = f(−x) 的函数，其图像关于 y 轴对称；在傅里叶分析中，偶函数可仅用余弦基函数表示，与之相对的奇函数（满足 f(x) = −f(−x)）则对应正弦基函数。

supporting_observations.support: 该观察明确将偶函数与余弦基函数关联，原文指出'you can represent any even function … with just the cosine basis'，并紧接着对比了奇函数与正弦特征的对应关系，为 definition 中傅里叶基表示及与奇函数比较的描述提供直接原文支持。

processed.definition: 奇函数（odd function）是关于原点反对称、满足 f(−x)=−f(x) 的函数。在线性方法构造基特征时，正弦类基函数的线性组合天然构成奇函数，与构成偶函数的余弦类基函数形成对照。

processed.definition: A cosine basis function is an individual cosine function of the form xi(s) = cos(π s^T c_i) that serves as a single feature in the Fourier cosine basis for linear function approximation. Its frequency along each state dimension is determined by the corresponding component of the integer vector c_i, with the full basis consisting of one such function for every possible choice of that integer vector.

supporting_observations.support: Provides the explicit form xi(s) = cos(π s^T c_i), defines c_i as an integer vector with components in {0, ..., n}, and states that the inner product s^T c_i assigns an integer to each dimension of s that determines the feature's frequency along that dimension, directly anchoring the mathematical identity and frequency semantics of a single cosine basis function.

Shows the feature in its one-dimensional usage (xi for i = 1, 2, 3, 4) for approximating functions over [0, 1], illustrating that each individual cosine function is a reusable building block rather than the entire basis.

Confirms that one feature is defined for each of the (n+1)^k possible integer vectors c_i, clarifying that a cosine basis function is a member of the full Fourier cosine basis set and not the basis itself.

processed.entity: Fourier cosine basis feature vector c_i
processed.definition: In the order-n Fourier cosine basis for a k-dimensional state, c_i is an integer index vector with components c_{ij} ∈ {0, …, n} that uniquely identifies the i-th basis feature via x_i(s) = cos(π s^T c_i), drawn from the (n+1)^k possible such vectors. A zero component makes the feature constant along the corresponding state dimension, a non-zero component introduces a frequency along that dimension, and the ratio of non-zero components determines the direction of any interaction between state variables.

supporting_observations.support: States the formal role of c_i = (c_{i1}, …, c_{ik})^T with c_{ij} ∈ {0, …, n}, the defining equation x_i(s) = cos(π s^T c_i), and that there are (n+1)^k such vectors — anchoring the integer-vector identity and the per-feature indexing.

The k = 2 example specifies that any zero in c yields constancy along that dimension, a non-zero entry sets a frequency, and the ratio of the two non-zero components gives the direction of the interaction — directly supporting the geometric interpretation in the second sentence.

processed.entity: Per-feature step-size parameter α_i (Fourier cosine features)
processed.definition: It is a per-feature step-size parameter α_i used in linear function approximation with Fourier cosine features, assigning each feature x_i its own learning rate rather than sharing a single global step-size α. Following Konidaris, Osentoski, and Thomas (2011), α_i is set to α divided by the Euclidean norm of the feature's coefficient vector √((c_{i1})² + ⋯ + (c_{ik})² (with the convention α_i = α when every c_{ij} = 0), in order to compensate for the different magnitudes of Fourier features at different frequencies.

supporting_observations.support: The sole observation provides the full canonical formula α_i = α / √((c_{i1})² + ⋯ + (c_{ik})²), the zero-coefficient exception (α_i = α when each c_{ij} = 0), the motivating rationale (compensating for differing feature magnitudes across frequencies), and the reference to Konidaris, Osentoski, and Thomas (2011) — all of which are directly anchored by P001182 from §9.5.2 Fourier Basis of Sutton & Barto.

processed.definition: A ringing artifact, also known as the Gibbs phenomenon, is an oscillation that appears in Fourier-series approximations near points of discontinuity, manifesting as persistent overshoot and ringing on either side of the jump. It is intrinsic to truncated Fourier representations and is difficult to suppress without including sufficiently high-frequency basis functions.

processed.definition: A discontinuity is a point at which a function is not continuous, representing a fundamental mathematical property of the function. In function approximation, discontinuities pose a challenge because approximations based on smooth basis functions (such as Fourier features) exhibit ringing oscillations near such points unless very high-frequency components are included.

supporting_observations.support: The source text directly defines discontinuities as points where a function is not continuous, and describes the causal consequence: Fourier features produce 'ringing' around these points unless very high frequency basis functions are included. processed.definition: A family of polynomial features used for linear function approximation, typically realized as the order-n polynomial basis over a k-dimensional state space, i.e., (n+1)^k features of the form ∏_{j=1..k} s_j^{c_{i,j}} with exponents c_{i,j} ∈ {0, 1, ..., n}.
