supporting_observations.support: Directly provides the recursion z_t = γλρ_t z_{t−1} + ∇q̂(S_t, A_t, w_t) (eq. 12.29), its derivation from the forward-view action-value λ-return (12.27) via the summation rule, the role of the importance-sampling ratio ρ_t, and its combination with the expectation-based TD error (12.28) and semi-gradient update to form Expected Sarsa(λ).

processed.entity: Off-policy λ-returns and eligibility traces via control variates
processed.definition: An importance-sampling-based framework in approximate reinforcement learning that constructs off-policy λ-returns and their corresponding eligibility traces by leveraging control variates, using the per-decision importance-sampling ratio ρ_t to derive both a state-value form and an action-value form. It produces the state TD error δ_t^s and the action-value TD error δ_t^a, and the action-value branch culminates in the Expected Sarsa(λ) algorithm.

supporting_observations.support: Directly anchors the framework's identity: it is an importance-sampling-based construction of off-policy λ-returns and eligibility traces using control variates, covers both state and action settings, derives the eligibility trace update (12.29) from the forward view, and ends with the Expected Sarsa(λ) algorithm.

Provides the historical attribution of off-policy eligibility traces (Precup et al., 2000, 2001; Bertsekas and Yu, 2009; Maei, 2011; Yu, 2012; Sutton, Mahmood, Precup, and van Hasselt, 2014) and explicitly notes that the section's presentation 'seems to be new' while confirming it ends with an elegant Expected Sarsa(λ) algorithm.

processed.definition: It is the second component of the challenge of off-policy learning, referring to the mismatch between the distribution over state–action pairs from which updates are actually drawn and the distribution that would be required to learn the target policy correctly. Off-policy eligibility traces correct for the expected value of the targets (the first part of the challenge) but do not address this distribution mismatch, which must be met instead by the algorithmic strategies surveyed in Section 12.11 of Sutton and Barto.

supporting_observations.support: The source text explicitly states that the challenge of off-policy learning has two parts, that off-policy eligibility traces handle the first part (correcting the expected value of targets) 'but not at all with the second part of the challenge, having to do with the distribution of updates,' and that meeting this second part requires the strategies summarized in Section 12.11 — directly anchoring the identity, role, and algorithmic consequence of this concept.

processed.definition: Watkins's Q(λ) is the original off-policy reinforcement learning algorithm proposed by Watkins (1989) to extend tabular Q-learning with eligibility traces, decaying traces in the usual way while a greedy action is taken and cutting them to zero after the first non-greedy action—a cutoff that can be implemented by temporarily setting λ to 0.

supporting_observations.support: Provides the core mechanism description: the original Q-learning-with-eligibility-traces method that decays traces normally under greedy actions and resets them after the first non-greedy action.

Attributes the algorithm to Watkins (1989), states the cutoff can be implemented by temporarily setting λ to 0, notes tabular-episodic-off-line convergence (Munos et al., 2016), and situates it among alternative Q(λ) algorithms by Peng & Williams and Sutton et al.
Index entry 'Q(λ), Watkins's, 312–314' confirms the canonical name, its status as a distinct algorithm, and the page range in the textbook where it is presented.

Index entry 'Q(λ), 312–314' shows the algorithm grouped with other off-policy eligibility-trace methods (Emphatic-TD, GQ, GTD, HTD, Tree Backup(λ)), supporting its classification as an off-policy RL algorithm.

processed.definition: Tree-Backup(λ), abbreviated TB(λ), is the eligibility-trace extension of the n-step Tree Backup algorithm in reinforcement learning, forming an off-policy learning method that avoids importance sampling and is regarded as the natural successor to Q-learning for combining off-policy learning with eligibility traces.

supporting_observations.support: Source text explicitly defines Tree-Backup(λ) as 'the eligibility trace version of Tree Backup,' notes that 'it can be applied to off-policy data,' and characterizes it as 'arguably the true successor to Q-learning because it retains its appealing absence of importance sampling,' directly anchoring every key claim in the definition.
Source text attributes Tree Backup(λ) to Precup, Sutton, and Singh (2000), anchoring its status as a named, originally proposed reinforcement learning algorithm distinct from ad hoc descriptions.

processed.definition: Off-policy data is experience or transition data generated by following a behavior policy that differs from the target policy that an algorithm is trying to evaluate or improve. It is the input required by off-policy reinforcement learning methods such as Tree-Backup(λ), although combining it with semi-gradient algorithms and a powerful function approximator does not guarantee stable learning.

processed.definition: λ is a scalar hyperparameter in [0, 1] that controls the degree of bootstrapping in TD(λ)-style reinforcement learning algorithms, serving as both the eligibility-trace decay rate in the backward view and the weight for combining n-step (or tree-backup) returns of different lengths in the forward view; in Tree-Backup(λ) it explicitly weights the tree-backup updates of each length, placing the method on a continuum from one-step TD (λ = 0) to Monte Carlo (λ = 1).

processed.definition: 它通常指不遵循贪心策略所选的动作，是贪心动作的互补概念。在 Watkins 的 Q(λ) 算法中，资格迹在遇到第一个非贪心动作时会被截断为零，从而终止该步的回溯序列（直到 episode 结束才结束）。

processed.definition: It is an approximator, such as a neural network, used in reinforcement learning to estimate value functions when exact tabular representation is infeasible. A powerful function approximator combined with off-policy data can cause semi-gradient methods such as TB(λ) to lose their stability guarantees.

processed.definition: HTD(λ) is a hybrid state-value reinforcement learning algorithm that combines aspects of GTD(λ) and TD(λ) for off-policy prediction with linear function approximation and eligibility traces. Its defining property is being a strict generalization of TD(λ) to off-policy learning—when the behavior and target policies coincide, HTD(λ) reduces exactly to TD(λ) (unlike GTD(λ))—and it augments the standard update with a second weight vector vt and a second set of behavior-policy accumulating eligibility traces z̄t.

supporting_observations.support: Provides the core identity of HTD(λ) as a hybrid state-value algorithm combining GTD(λ) and TD(λ), its strict-generalization property under on-policy conditions, and the specific mechanism (second weight vector vt, second eligibility traces z̄t, auxiliary step-size parameter β) that enables the reduction to TD(λ).

Cross-references HTD(λ) within the index of off-policy methods with eligibility traces alongside GQ(λ), GTD(λ), and Emphatic-TD(λ), confirming its placement in the family of off-policy linear-function-approximation trace methods.

processed.definition: Emphatic TD(λ) is an off-policy temporal-difference reinforcement learning algorithm that extends the one-step Emphatic-TD method to eligibility traces, using an emphatic weighting (via an emphasis Mt and followon trace Ft) to reweight its updates. Compared with ordinary TD(λ), it preserves strong off-policy convergence guarantees for any state-dependent bootstrapping function λ and any degree of bootstrapping, but typically exhibits high variance and potentially slow convergence.

processed.definition: one-step Emphatic-TD is the one-step (non-trace) variant of the Emphatic Temporal-Difference learning algorithm, presented in Sections 9.11 and 11.8 of Sutton and Barto's 'Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction.' processed.entity: Average feature vector x̄_t (target-policy expectation, reinforcement learning)
processed.definition: In reinforcement learning, the average feature vector x̄_t is a state-level feature representation defined as the expectation of state–action feature vectors under the target policy at that state, x̄t = Σa π(a|St)x(St, a). It is introduced in the GQ(λ) algorithm, where it appears in the update of the secondary weight vector w_t and in computing the expectation form of the TD error.

processed.definition: In the Emphatic TD(λ) algorithm, the followon trace F_t is an auxiliary trace variable defined recursively by F_t = ρ_{t-1}γ_t F_{t-1} + I_t (with F_0 = i(S_0)). It is combined with the interest I_t to form the emphasis M_t that reweights the eligibility trace in the weight update.

processed.definition: Accumulating eligibility traces are a conventional form of eligibility trace in reinforcement learning in which the trace value for each active feature is incremented by 1 on every visit (z_i ← z_i + 1), rather than being reset to 1 as in replacing traces. They are the standard trace mechanism used in conventional TD(λ) and Sarsa(λ), serving as the baseline against which replacing traces and dutch traces are contrasted.

processed.definition: Yu's counterexample is a theoretical counterexample, attributed to Ghiassian, Rafiee, and Sutton (2016), demonstrating that conventional TD(λ) is not guaranteed to converge for all state-dependent λ (bootstrapping parameters that depend on the state). processed.definition: In temporal-difference (TD) learning with eligibility traces, the trace-decay/bootstrapping parameter λ when it is allowed to vary as a function of state rather than being held at a fixed constant. processed.definition: In reinforcement learning, the forward view is a theoretical perspective that formulates a learning algorithm by looking forward from each visited state to future rewards and states to determine how to compute the update target. processed.definition: The Options framework is a reinforcement learning formalism for temporal abstraction, introduced by Sutton, Precup, and Singh (1999) with precursors in Sutton (1995a) and Parr (1998), in which temporally extended courses of action (options) are formalized as an internal policy together with a state-dependent termination function. An option ω = ⟨π_ω, β_ω⟩ generalizes a primitive action—low-level actions are special cases whose termination function is zero—and the framework underlies hierarchical learning and planning over multi-step behaviors.

processed.definition: REINFORCE is a classical Monte Carlo policy-gradient algorithm (Williams, 1992) that updates the policy parameter at time t using only the action actually taken, scaled by the complete return from that time. It is defined only for the episodic case, performs all updates retrospectively after the episode ends, and as a pure Monte Carlo method can exhibit high variance—issues later addressed by extensions such as REINFORCE with baseline and one-step actor–critic methods.

supporting_observations.support: Anchors the core identity: classical REINFORCE (Williams, 1992), update involves only A_t, uses the complete return G_t, is a Monte Carlo algorithm, and is well defined only for the episodic case with retrospective updates.
Provides the convergence guarantee as a stochastic gradient method and explicitly notes the high-variance / slow-learning drawback of REINFORCE as a Monte Carlo method.
Identifies REINFORCE as a Monte Carlo method for learning the policy parameter θ using ∇ln π(A_t|S_t,θ), and clarifies that REINFORCE with baseline is a strict generalization (baseline may be zero).
Distinguishes REINFORCE by its use of the full return, contrasted with one-step actor–critic methods that replace the full return with the one-step return.

States that REINFORCE follows directly from the policy gradient theorem and that adding a state-value baseline reduces its variance without introducing bias; also credits Williams (1987, 1992) and cites convergence proofs by Phansalkar and Thathachar (1995).

processed.definition: The REINFORCE update is the policy-parameter update rule θ_{t+1} = θ_t + α G_t ∇π(A_t|St,θ_t)/π(A_t|St,θ_t) (Sutton & Barto, equation 13.8) used in Monte Carlo policy gradient methods. Each step moves the parameter vector in the direction that most increases the probability of repeating the action actually taken, with a step size proportional to the return G_t and inversely proportional to that action's probability.

supporting_observations.support: Provides the exact equation (13.8), the proportionality to G_t and to the score-like vector ∇π/π, and the interpretation that the vector points in the direction in parameter space that most increases the probability of repeating A_t.

processed.definition: It is a policy-gradient algorithm whose update rule sums the gradient contribution over all actions at the current state, using a learned approximation q̂ to the action-value function, rather than using only the single action actually taken. Presented as equation 13.7 in Sutton & Barto's textbook and first proposed by Sutton, Singh, and McAllester (2000), it is also known in later literature as 'expected policy gradients' and 'mean actor critic' and is explicitly contrasted with REINFORCE.

processed.definition: The eligibility vector is the score-function vector ∇ ln π(A_t|S_t, θ) that appears in the REINFORCE policy-gradient update, and is mathematically equivalent to the ratio ∇π(A_t|S_t,θ)/π(A_t|S_t,θ) via the identity ∇ ln x = ∇x/x. In the REINFORCE algorithm it is the sole place where the dependence of the parameterized policy on its parameters θ enters the update, and it is distinct from the eligibility traces used in TD(λ) methods despite the shared terminology.

supporting_observations.support: The passage from §13.3 of Sutton & Barto (2nd ed.) directly defines the eligibility vector as ∇ ln π(A_t|S_t, θ), notes its equivalence to the fractional form via ∇ ln x = ∇x/x, and states that it is 'the only place that the policy parameterization appears in the algorithm,' all of which anchor both the mathematical identity and the role of the quantity in REINFORCE.

processed.definition: Monte Carlo methods are a class of reinforcement learning algorithms that learn value estimates or policies directly from sampled experience rather than from a complete model of the environment. They are characterized by using the complete return from each visited state and performing all updates retrospectively after an episode terminates, which makes them inherently episodic.

processed.definition: REINFORCE with Baseline is a policy gradient algorithm that generalizes REINFORCE by subtracting a state-dependent baseline b(s) from the return G_t in the update rule θ_{t+1} = θ_t + α(G_t − b(S_t))∇ln π(A_t|St, θ_t), and is therefore a strict generalization of REINFORCE because a uniformly zero baseline recovers the original update. It is an episodic Monte Carlo method that uses two step sizes—α^θ for the policy parameter and α^w for a separately learned state-value function used as the baseline—and, unlike actor–critic methods, the baseline is formed before the transition's action and so does not assess that action.

Anchors the learned state-value function's role as a baseline and the distinguishing property that the baseline is formed before the transition's action and cannot assess it, separating REINFORCE with Baseline from actor–critic methods.

processed.definition: In policy gradient methods, the baseline b(s) is a function or random variable subtracted from the return or action value in the gradient update that is independent of the action a, so that it leaves the expected value of the update unchanged while often substantially reducing its variance. processed.definition: One-step actor–critic methods are actor–critic policy-gradient algorithms that replace the full Monte Carlo return of REINFORCE with the one-step return and use a learned state-value function as a baseline; they are the actor–critic analog of one-step TD methods such as TD(0), Sarsa(0), and Q-learning, are fully online and incremental, and avoid the complexities of eligibility traces.

processed.definition: Ivan Pavlov was a celebrated Russian physiologist best known for his studies of the digestive system in dogs, during which he discovered that an animal's innate responses (such as salivation) can come to be elicited by previously neutral stimuli (such as a metronome) that have been repeatedly paired with the original trigger. This finding is the foundation of classical (Pavlovian) conditioning, the learning paradigm in which a conditioned stimulus comes to evoke a conditioned response through its association with an unconditioned stimulus.

supporting_observations.support: 该观察直接给出 'the celebrated Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov'，并描述其研究消化系统、在狗身上通过巴甫洛夫铃声（节拍器）与食物配对实验发现条件反射，从而奠定 classical (Pavlovian) conditioning 的全部核心事实，均与 definition 一致。

processed.definition: An unconditioned response (UR) is an innate, unlearned reflex that is naturally and reliably elicited by an unconditioned stimulus (US) without any prior training, such as salivation in response to food in Pavlov's classical-conditioning paradigm. It serves as the natural baseline reaction that a learned conditioned response (CR) is built upon when a previously neutral stimulus comes to predict the US.

supporting_observations.support: The passage directly defines URs as 'inborn responses (e.g., salivation …) "unconditioned responses" (URs)' naturally triggered by 'unconditioned stimuli (e.g., food),' anchoring the core meaning as an innate, unlearned reaction to its natural triggering stimulus. It also situates the UR opposite the conditioned response (CR) in the classical-conditioning framework, supporting the second sentence's contrast.

processed.definition: An unconditioned stimulus (US) is a biologically effective stimulus in classical (Pavlovian) conditioning that naturally elicits an unconditioned response without prior learning, as exemplified by food triggering salivation in Pavlov's experiments. It is also called a reinforcer because pairing it with a previously neutral cue enables that conditioned stimulus to evoke a conditioned response, and unlike an instrumental reinforcer it is delivered independently of the animal's behavior.

supporting_observations.support: Provides the core definition: US is a natural triggering stimulus (e.g., food) that elicits an unconditioned response, and is called a reinforcer because it reinforces producing a CR in response to the CS. Anchors the food example and the US–CS–CR relationship in delay conditioning.

Establishes the defining contrast with instrumental conditioning: in classical conditioning the US is delivered independently of the animal's behavior, distinguishing it from an operant reinforcer that is contingent on behavior.

Shows that the same US concept is used in the TD/dopamine reward-prediction-error model, where it corresponds functionally to the onset of a non-zero reward signal that terminates the internal stimulus sequence, confirming the cross-section use of the term as the reward-predicting event in classical conditioning.

processed.definition: In classical (Pavlovian) conditioning, a conditioned response (CR) is a learned reaction—originally elicited only by an unconditioned stimulus (US)—that comes to be triggered by a previously neutral conditioned stimulus (CS) once the animal has learned that the CS predicts the US (e.g., salivation to a metronome). Its timing, shape, and trial-by-trial development depend on the species, the response system being measured, and the parameters of the conditioning trials, and in many cases the magnitude or probability of the CR grows as the expected time of the US approaches.

supporting_observations.support: Anchors the core meaning of the CR: a 'new response triggered by predictive stimuli (e.g., here also salivation)' in classical conditioning, produced after the animal learns that the CS predicts the US; also introduces the reinforcing role of the US in producing a CR to the CS.

Anchors the second sentence's claims about CR properties: timing, shape, and development over trials depend on the species, response system, and conditioning parameters; the CR's magnitude/probability increases as the expected time of the US approaches; concrete example of the rabbit nictitating-membrane CR.

processed.definition: A conditioned stimulus (CS) is a initially neutral stimulus in classical conditioning that does not normally elicit a strong response, but, after repeated pairing with an unconditioned stimulus (US), comes to predict it and triggers a learned conditioned response. It is typically contrasted with the unconditioned stimulus (which innately elicits a response) and is studied in both behavioral experiments and in neural recordings (e.g., dopamine neuron firing) where the CS comes to substitute for the primary reward.

supporting_observations.support: Directly anchors the core definition: a initially neutral stimulus (e.g., the metronome sound) that becomes a CS once the animal learns it predicts the US and so produces a CR. Also supplies the standard contrast with the unconditioned stimulus and the origin of the US being called a 'reinforcer'.

Confirms the same construct in a neuroscience context, showing that the CS 'predicts reward' and that dopamine neurons 'respond to a conditioned stimulus (CS) that predicts reward and do not respond to the reward itself'—i.e., the CS has acquired the response-eliciting role of the US, consistent with the classical-conditioning definition.

processed.definition: Delay conditioning is a type of classical conditioning paradigm in which the conditioned stimulus (CS) extends throughout the interstimulus interval (ISI), with the CS and unconditioned stimulus (US) co-terminating in the common version depicted. It is distinguished from trace conditioning, where the US begins only after the CS has already ended, leaving a trace interval between the two stimuli.

supporting_observations.support: The source passage directly defines delay conditioning as a classical conditioning experiment in which the CS extends throughout the ISI, with the CS ending when the US ends, and explicitly contrasts it with trace conditioning, where the US begins after the CS ends and the gap is called the trace interval. The figure and model_quote in P002071/P002072 anchor both the temporal structure of the paradigm and the trace-vs-delay distinction.

processed.definition: Trace conditioning is a classical (Pavlovian) conditioning paradigm in which the unconditioned stimulus (US) begins after the conditioned stimulus (CS) has ended, leaving a temporal gap between them. The interval between CS offset and US onset is called the trace interval, and the paradigm takes its name from the persistent neural trace of the CS that Pavlov proposed enables learning across this gap.

supporting_observations.support: Directly defines trace conditioning as the classical conditioning arrangement in which the US begins after the CS ends, and explicitly names the time between CS offset and US onset as the trace interval; also establishes trace conditioning as a sibling paradigm to delay conditioning within classical conditioning.

Provides the mechanistic justification for the paradigm's name and existence: Pavlov (1927) proposed that every stimulus leaves a persistent trace in the nervous system, and that learning in trace conditioning occurs through the simultaneous presence of that CS trace and the US when there is a temporal gap between CS offset and US onset.

processed.definition: The interstimulus interval (ISI) is the time interval between the onset of the conditioned stimulus (CS) and the onset of the unconditioned stimulus (US) in classical conditioning. The rate and effectiveness of conditioning learning depend on this interval, and in delay conditioning the CS typically extends throughout it, which distinguishes ISI from the trace interval in trace conditioning where the CS ends before the US begins.

supporting_observations.support: Directly defines ISI as the time interval between the CS onset and the US onset, provides the alias 'ISI', and situates the concept within delay conditioning while contrasting it with the trace interval used in trace conditioning.

Reaffirms that ISI is the interval between the onsets of the CS and the US (confirming 'Inter-stimulus interval' as a hyphenation variant of the same term) and adds the empirical fact that the rate and effectiveness of conditioning learning depend on this interval.

processed.definition: Trace interval is the temporal gap between the offset of the conditioned stimulus (CS) and the onset of the unconditioned stimulus (US) in the trace conditioning paradigm of classical conditioning. It marks the stimulus-free separation that distinguishes trace conditioning from delay conditioning, in which the CS and US overlap or co-terminate.

supporting_observations.support: The source text explicitly defines the trace interval as 'the time interval between CS offset and US onset' and frames it within trace conditioning, where 'the US begins after the CS ends'; the same passage contrasts this with the interstimulus interval (ISI) used when 'the CS ending [coincides with] when the US ends,' anchoring the contrast with delay-style procedures that motivates the second sentence of the definition.

processed.definition: A nictitating membrane is a protective inner (third) eyelid present in many animals that can be drawn across the eye to shield it. In classical conditioning research, its closure in the rabbit serves as the unconditioned response to an air puff delivered to the eye and can become a conditioned response anticipating that puff.

supporting_observations.support: The source text explicitly calls it 'a protective inner eyelid called the nictitating membrane' in the rabbit, identifies its closure as the UR to an air-puff US, and states that after conditioning 'the tone comes to trigger a CR consisting of membrane closure that begins before the air puff,' directly anchoring both the anatomical description and the conditioning role.

processed.definition: Blocking is a phenomenon in classical conditioning in which, after an animal has already learned that one conditioned stimulus (CS) predicts an unconditioned stimulus (US), a new CS added to the original as a compound CS fails to gain associative strength, so it elicits little or no conditioned response (CR) when later presented alone. First reported by Kamin (1968) and commonly called Kamin blocking, it is a central result explained by the Rescorla–Wagner model and historically challenged the view that temporal contiguity alone is sufficient for conditioning.

supporting_observations.support: Provides the canonical description of blocking (prior CS learning blocks learning to a new compound CS) and a concrete rabbit nictitating-membrane conditioning example, anchoring the core mechanism of the definition.

Supplies the Rescorla–Wagner mechanistic account: the aggregate associative strength already approximates the US-supported level, so the added CS introduces little prediction error and little new learning—supporting the 'blocked' characterization in the definition.

Anchors blocking's theoretical significance: it showed that a mechanistic, contiguity-based model could account for the effect without invoking complex cognitive mechanisms, supporting the definition's claim that blocking challenged pure contiguity theories.

Restates the standard blocking result (a newly added CS fails to gain associative strength when a CS already predicts the US) and notes the temporal-primacy boundary condition, confirming the identity of the phenomenon across model simulations.
Provides the historical attribution: Kamin (1968) first reported blocking in classical conditioning, establishing 'Kamin blocking' as the standard name used in the definition.

processed.definition: Higher-order conditioning is a phenomenon in classical conditioning in which a previously conditioned stimulus (CS) comes to serve as an unconditioned stimulus (US) that conditions another initially neutral stimulus, first demonstrated by Pavlov with his metronome-to-black-square dog experiment. It encompasses second-order conditioning and can extend to third-order and beyond, and is typically discussed in contrast to related effects such as blocking and in relation to whether trial-level models like Rescorla–Wagner can account for it.

supporting_observations.support: Provides the core definition (a previously-conditioned CS acts as a US for a new neutral stimulus) and cites Pavlov's original dog experiment — metronome predicting food, then a black square paired with the metronome without food — as the founding demonstration of the phenomenon.

Reaffirms the core definition and extends it to third-order conditioning and beyond; explicitly places higher-order conditioning beyond the scope of trial-level models like Rescorla–Wagner and illustrates the TD model's account with the second-order conditioning simulation in Figure 14.3.

Identifies higher-order conditioning as including second-order, third-order, and conditioned-reinforcement cases, and notes that the TD model extends the Rescorla–Wagner model to address how it arises.

Confirms it as a classical conditioning phenomenon and contrasts the Rescorla–Wagner model (no mechanism for it) with the TD model (emerges naturally from the bootstrapping idea underlying TD algorithms).

Adds the empirical observation that higher-order conditioning beyond second-order is rarely seen in experiments, while TD-style learning is not so limited — an additional identifying feature about the empirical scope of the phenomenon.

processed.definition: Second-order conditioning is a form of higher-order classical conditioning in which a stimulus already trained to predict a reinforcing unconditioned stimulus (US) itself acts as a secondary US, thereby conditioning a response to a new, initially neutral conditioned stimulus (CS). It demonstrates that learned predictors of reinforcement can themselves acquire reinforcing properties, and is distinguished from first-order conditioning by the absence of the original primary US during the critical pairing trials.

supporting_observations.support: Provides the canonical example (metronome sound → black square CS, salivation CR) and explicitly identifies second-order conditioning as a subtype of higher-order conditioning, distinguishing it from third-order conditioning.

Details the two-phase procedure: CSB first trained to predict the US, then paired with a new CSA in the absence of the US so that CSA acquires associative strength via secondary reinforcement; also notes the extinction-based difficulty of sustaining higher-order conditioning and its connection to TD-model bootstrapping.

Articulates the abstract principle underlying the phenomenon—'predictors of reinforcing stimuli become reinforcing themselves'—which is the chapter's summary characterization of second-order conditioning.

Cites empirical work (Gibbs et al., 1991) on second-order conditioning of the rabbit nictitating membrane response, anchoring the concept in a well-known animal preparation beyond the textbook's running example.
Bibliographic entry for Gibbs et al. (1991), corroborating that second-order conditioning is a recognized experimental paradigm in the animal learning literature.

processed.definition: Third-order conditioning is a higher-order classical conditioning procedure in which a stimulus that already functions as a second-order conditioned stimulus (CS) is used as an unconditioned stimulus (US) to establish a conditioned response (CR) to a new, otherwise neutral CS. It represents the third level in a chain of higher-order conditioning (beyond first- and second-order) and is especially difficult to demonstrate, because the higher-order reinforcer tends to lose its reinforcing value without repeated pairing with the original US.

supporting_observations.support: P002077 explicitly describes third-order conditioning as a further extension of higher-order conditioning in which a second-order CS (e.g., the black square) is used as a US to establish salivation CRs to another neutral CS, and notes that higher-order conditioning is difficult to demonstrate above second order because a higher-order reinforcer loses its reinforcing value when not repeatedly followed by the original US.

processed.definition: The Rescorla–Wagner model is an influential trial-level model of classical (Pavlovian) conditioning, proposed by Rescorla and Wagner in 1972, in which learning is driven by a prediction-error or 'surprise' signal that updates the associative strength of each component stimulus of a compound CS. It was developed primarily to account for blocking and is widely treated as a foundational error-correction rule against which later models, such as the TD model, are compared.

supporting_observations.support: Introduces the Rescorla–Wagner model (Rescorla and Wagner, 1972) as an influential explanation for blocking within a classical-conditioning discussion, anchoring the authorship, year, and primary purpose.

States the core mechanism—that learning occurs only when the animal is surprised (expectations are violated)—and describes the associative-strength update based on aggregate strength and prediction error, anchoring the mechanistic description in the definition.
Establishes the model as a trial-level rule (one step = one trial) that does not model within-trial or between-trial timing, anchoring the 'trial-level' characterization in the definition.
Labels the model 'influential' and states that the TD model 'generalizes' it by including the temporal dimension, supporting the typical-comparison aspect of the definition.
Reaffirms the core 'learning when surprised' idea and traces it to Kamin (1969), reinforcing the mechanistic claim with an independent passage.

processed.definition: It is a real-time temporal-difference (TD) model of classical conditioning that extends the trial-level Rescorla–Wagner rule by replacing trial-level updates with bootstrapping TD errors over within-trial time steps, effectively a semi-gradient-descent TD(λ) learning rule with linear function approximation. Compared with the Rescorla–Wagner model, it naturally accounts for the anticipatory timing of conditioned responses, ISI-dependent learning, serial compounds, higher-order conditioning, and blocking phenomena such as temporal primacy overriding blocking.

supporting_observations.support: Anchors the canonical identity: the model 'uses the bootstrapping idea… to extend the Rescorla–Wagner model's account of blocking to include both the anticipatory nature of CRs and higher-order conditioning.'

Confirms the model 'extends the Rescorla–Wagner model to address how within-trial and between-trial timing relationships among stimuli can influence learning and how higher-order conditioning might arise,' supporting the real-time/timing and higher-order aspects of the definition.

Establishes the 'real-time model' identity (vs. trial-level), the within/between-trial time-step reframing, and the bootstrapping basis for higher-order conditioning, directly supporting the first sentence of the definition.

Provides concrete predictions (temporal primacy overriding blocking, Egger–Miller effect, second-order conditioning) that illustrate the 'phenomena beyond trial-level models' clause in the second sentence, all attributed to the bootstrapping/backing-up idea.
Identifies the model as 'basically the semi-gradient-descent TD(λ) algorithm with linear function approximation,' directly anchoring the algorithmic characterization in the first sentence.

processed.entity: 初级强化（动物学习心理学）
processed.definition: 初级强化是动物学习心理学中的一类强化过程，其奖赏或惩罚效价由动物神经系统经进化内置，无需学习即可直接增强或抑制行为；与通过预测初级强化而获得价值的次级（条件性）强化相对，在强化学习算法中通常对应即时奖赏信号 R_{t+1}。

supporting_observations.support: 给出核心定义'其奖赏/惩罚性质由进化内置'，并以高级条件化为背景将初级强化与次级/条件性强化进行区分
具体说明进化内置的奖赏机制（营养食物的味道、性接触、成功逃脱等示例），并界定次级奖赏为直接预测初级奖赏的奖赏
在 Hull 的延迟强化理论中，初级强化作为刺激痕迹调节下的基础奖赏信号，与条件性强化共同构成目标梯度
在 TD 误差 δ_t 分解中将 R_{t+1} 明确定义为'初级强化贡献'，并指出当 V(S_{t+1})−V(S_t)=0 时 δ_t 即'纯'初级强化信号

processed.entity: 次级强化（动物学习心理学）
processed.definition: 次级强化（也称条件性强化、条件强化）是指由原本中性、但因能够预测初级强化（其奖赏/惩罚效力由动物进化内置）而获得强化效力的刺激所传递的强化效应；它既涵盖直接预测初级强化的二级强化，也包括通过预测其他次级强化刺激而间接预测初级强化的更高阶（higher-order）强化。该概念是动物学习心理学中用于解释延迟强化下学习行为的关键现象，并对应于强化学习中价值函数所提供的近乎即时的评价反馈。

supporting_observations.support: 原文核心定义：始终预测初级强化的刺激成为次级强化物（secondary reinforcer），它传递的即次级/条件性强化；这是当前实体最直接的来源依据。
明确将 conditioned reinforcement 与 secondary reinforcement 等同，定义其作为学习现象（传递条件性奖赏/惩罚，作用类似初级强化），为该实体的同义关系提供原文支持。
将 conditioned reinforcement 锚定到 Hull（1943）的目标梯度理论，解释其在延迟强化中的作用机制（向后传递、延长梯度），为定义中'解释延迟强化下学习行为'的补充提供出处。
将次级强化与强化学习中的价值函数直接对应（提供近乎即时的评价反馈），为定义中'对应于价值函数'的比较关系提供原文支持。
给出'higher-order reward'的规范定义：直接或间接预测初级奖赏的刺激所传递的奖赏，区分了 higher-order（一般概念）与 secondary（直接预测的特例），为定义中'涵盖更高阶强化'的范围声明提供支持。

processed.definition: Higher-order instrumental conditioning is a form of instrumental conditioning in which a stimulus that consistently predicts primary reinforcement itself acquires reinforcing value, becoming a conditioned (secondary or higher-order) reinforcer that increases the likelihood of behavior leading to it. It is analogously realized in actor–critic reinforcement learning methods, where the critic's TD value estimates supply moment-by-moment conditioned reinforcement to the actor, helping address delayed credit assignment.

supporting_observations.support: Anchors the core mechanism: a stimulus consistently predicting primary reinforcement becomes a reinforcer itself (a secondary/conditioned/higher-order reinforcer), and conditioned reinforcement acts like primary reinforcement in strengthening behavior that produces it.

Anchors the concrete learning-system analog: in actor–critic methods the critic's TD value estimates provide conditioned reinforcement to the actor, supporting learning when the primary reward is delayed, which is how higher-order instrumental conditioning is operationalized in RL.

processed.definition: Temporal contiguity in classical conditioning is the principle that close temporal succession of an unconditioned stimulus (US) following a conditioned stimulus (CS) is both a necessary and sufficient condition for associative learning to occur. It is a contiguity-based view of conditioning that was challenged by blocking results and later revised by the Rescorla–Wagner model.

supporting_observations.support: Passage P002076 directly states the core claim—'a necessary and sufficient condition for conditioning is that a US frequently follows a CS closely in time'—and explicitly identifies blocking results as what challenged this temporal-contiguity view, anchoring both the definition and its historical status.

Passage P002097 re-expresses the same idea as 'traditional contiguity theories of conditioning—that temporal contiguity of stimuli was a necessary and sufficient condition for learning,' confirming the identity of the concept and documenting that the Rescorla–Wagner model provided the revised account of blocking.

processed.definition: It is a scalar variable in the Rescorla–Wagner model, assigned to each component stimulus of a compound conditioned stimulus, that quantifies how reliably that component predicts the unconditioned stimulus. Its value is updated trial-by-trial via the model's prediction-error rule, with the model assuming that larger values produce stronger or more likely conditioned responses while negative values mean no conditioned response occurs.

supporting_observations.support: Directly defines associative strength in the Rescorla–Wagner model: a number representing how strongly or reliably a component stimulus of a compound CS is predictive of a US, updated via aggregate associative strength, and mapped such that larger V produces stronger/more likely CRs and negative V produces no CR.

Shows that 'associative strength' is the shared term used to denote the learned predictive weight across models, confirming that the quantity discussed for Rescorla–Wagner is the same conceptual object (typically denoted V) later compared with the TD model.

processed.definition: A compound conditioned stimulus (compound CS) is a conditioned stimulus made up of several component stimuli (e.g., A and X) that are presented together in a single classical conditioning trial. In the Rescorla–Wagner model, the associative strength of each component is updated according to the aggregate associative strength of the entire compound rather than according to the strength of that component alone.

supporting_observations.support: Passages P002083–P002084 are the primary source: they explicitly define a compound CS as a stimulus consisting of several component stimuli presented together in a classical conditioning trial, introduce the worked example 'AX', and state that each component's associative strength changes in a way that depends on the aggregate associative strength of the whole stimulus compound — directly anchoring both sentences of the definition.

The index entry 'compound stimulus, 345, 346–356, 371, 382' confirms that the term is used in the classical-conditioning chapter (pages 345–356) and is cross-referenced with blocking, the Rescorla–Wagner model, and the TD model, supporting the identification of the entity as a classical-conditioning construct and corroborating the 'compound stimulus' alias.

processed.definition: In the Rescorla–Wagner model of classical conditioning, the aggregate associative strength is the total associative strength assigned to an entire compound conditioned stimulus, defined as the sum of the associative strengths of its individual component stimuli (e.g., V_AX = V_A + V_X). It serves as the animal's trial-level expectation of the unconditioned stimulus, against which prediction error (surprise) is computed when updating each component's strength, and corresponds to a value estimate or US prediction in reinforcement learning terms.

supporting_observations.support: Provides the core definition: aggregate associative strength is associated with the entire compound CS, V_AX = V_A + V_X, and component strengths are updated with respect to this aggregate quantity.
Anchors the 'US prediction' / value-estimate interpretation and clarifies that the aggregate associative strength is the expectation violated by the prediction error (surprise) on each trial.

Confirms the same weighted-sum definition (equation 14.1) is reused for the aggregate associative strength in the TD model, supporting its identity as a general compound-level prediction quantity beyond a single trial context.

processed.entity: asymptotic level of associative strength (Rescorla–Wagner model)
processed.definition: In the Rescorla–Wagner model of classical conditioning, the asymptotic level of associative strength (denoted R_Y) is the maximum associative strength that a given unconditioned stimulus (US) can support, serving as the target value toward which the aggregate associative strength V_AX converges. Once V_AX reaches this level, the prediction error R_Y − V_AX becomes zero and further conditioning trials produce no further change in the component associative strengths—an assumption that accounts for blocking.

supporting_observations.support: The source text explicitly defines R_Y as 'the asymptotic level of associative strength that the US Y can support' and identifies it as a Rescorla–Wagner model parameter on which the step-size parameters depend, anchoring the core meaning of the entity.

The same observation describes the convergence mechanism: as long as V_AX is below R_Y the prediction error is positive and component strengths increase; when V_AX equals R_Y, the strengths stop changing, and this zero-error state is what makes blocking occur when a new component is added. This directly supports the second sentence of the definition.

processed.definition: A trial-level model is a temporal-granularity characteristic of the Rescorla–Wagner model of classical conditioning, specifying that it updates associative strengths only at the boundary between successive trials rather than describing any within-trial or inter-trial dynamics. This is what distinguishes it from a full TD model, which explicitly represents how states change during a trial.

supporting_observations.support: The passage directly defines the Rescorla–Wagner model as a trial-level model, stating it 'deals with how associative strengths change from trial to trial without considering any details about what happens within and between trials,' and contrasts this with the full TD model that considers how states change during a trial.

processed.definition: From a machine learning perspective, the Rescorla–Wagner model is an error-correction supervised learning rule that adjusts its weights (associative strengths) by an amount proportional to a prediction error, and is essentially equivalent to the Least Mean Square (LMS) / Widrow–Hoff learning rule, making it a curve-fitting or regression algorithm.

supporting_observations.support: The source text directly states that 'From the perspective of machine learning, the Rescorla–Wagner model is an error-correction supervised learning rule' and that it is 'essentially the same as the Least Mean Square (LMS), or Widrow–Hoff, learning rule,' anchoring both the identity of this entity as the ML characterization of the R–W model and its equivalence to the LMS/Widrow–Hoff rule.

processed.definition: A response-generation mechanism in the Rescorla–Wagner model is a component that maps the model's associative strengths V to conditioned responses (CRs), translating learned values into observable behavior. Rescorla and Wagner did not specify a concrete mapping but assumed that larger V's produce stronger or more likely CRs, while negative V's produce no CRs, leaving the exact form dependent on the experimental situation.

supporting_observations.support: The primary source explicitly defines the component as a 'way of mapping values of V's to CRs' needed to complete the Rescorla–Wagner model, and states Rescorla and Wagner's assumptions about larger V's producing stronger/more likely CRs and negative V's producing none.

Demonstrates that the same conceptual role—translating internal values/predictions into CR profiles—appears in the TD model simulations, confirming the mechanism is a general component type rather than something unique to the R-W model.

processed.entity: Semi-gradient TD(λ) with linear function approximation
processed.definition: 半梯度 TD(λ) 是 TD(λ) 的函数逼近版本（见 Sutton & Barto 第 12 章），在线性函数逼近下以值梯度 ∇v̂(S_t, w_t) 通过资格迹逐步增量更新权重向量 w，可应用于回合式与持续性任务；其使用资格迹的反向视图（backward view）经验上逼近基于 λ-回报的前向视图（forward view），但因更新目标含当前权重故为'半梯度'而非完整梯度下降。

supporting_observations.support: 直接给出该算法为 TD(λ) 的函数逼近形式（'the semi-gradient version of TD(λ) with function approximation'），说明其使用值梯度 ∇v̂(S_t, w_t) 通过资格迹逐步更新权重向量，并给出带策略 π、步长 α>0、衰减率 λ∈[0,1] 的伪代码；明确其可应用于持续性任务。
明确限定为'with linear function approximation (Chapter 12)'，并陈述其反向视图（backward view）的存在；关于 TD 模型中 R_t 不必是奖励信号的差异是该算法被应用于经典条件作用模型时的具体说明，不构成算法本身身份边界。
在第 15 章再次以'semi-gradient-descent TD(λ) algorithm with linear function approximation'指代同一算法，并将其作为经典条件作用 TD 模型的基础，验证该算法作为独立实体的稳定身份。

processed.definition: Trial-level models are a class of classical conditioning models, exemplified by the Rescorla–Wagner model, that treat each conditioning trial as a single discrete event without tracking within-trial temporal structure. Unlike real-time models such as the TD model, they cannot represent the timing and durations of CSs and USs, the inter-stimulus interval (ISI), serial compounds, or the temporal profile of conditioned responses (CRs).

supporting_observations.support: Passage P002112 explicitly contrasts 'trial-level models' with 'real-time conditioning models like the TD model' and lists the four representational limitations (timing/durations of CSs and USs, ISI, serial compounds, temporal profile of CRs). processed.definition: A type of compound conditioned stimulus (CS) in classical conditioning in which the component stimuli occur in a sequential temporal order rather than all beginning and ending at the same time, and which is used to study timing-dependent phenomena such as the facilitation of remote associations between earlier components and the US.

processed.definition: Presence representation is a stimulus representation used in the TD model of classical conditioning, in which each component conditioned stimulus (CS) on a trial is encoded by a single binary feature that takes value 1 whenever that component is present and 0 otherwise. It is the simplest of three representations (alongside the complete serial compound and microstimulus representations) and assumes complete temporal generalization across a CS's duration, so the model learns only one weight per stimulus, yielding an approximately constant US prediction while the CS is on and limiting its ability to reproduce features of conditioned-response timing.

supporting_observations.support: Anchors the formal definition (one binary feature per component CS, value 1 when present and 0 otherwise), identifies it as one of three TD-model stimulus representations (CSC, MS, presence), and supplies the comparison of temporal generalization along which the three representations differ.

Provides the behavioral consequence that the TD model with presence representation learns only one weight per stimulus, producing a nearly constant US prediction during the CS, and explicitly states the limitation that it cannot recreate many features of CR timing.

processed.definition: A tapped delay line is an engineering signal-processing structure in which the onset of an input signal generates a sequence of time-shifted internal signals at regular, precisely timed intervals along a delay path. In the reinforcement-learning literature on classical conditioning, it is used as an analogy to characterize representations (such as the CSC representation) in which an external stimulus triggers a cascade of precisely timed short-duration internal signals that persists for the stimulus's duration.

supporting_observations.support: The source text explicitly states that 'it is what engineers call a "tapped delay line"' and describes it in the context of the CSC representation as a structure where 'the onset of each external stimulus initiates a sequence of precisely-timed short-duration internal signals that continues until the external stimulus ends.' processed.entity: Temporal generalization gradient (TD model of classical conditioning)
processed.definition: In the TD model of classical conditioning, it is the conceptual dimension along which different stimulus representations are ordered by how much they force generalization among nearby time points, ranging from no generalization (complete serial compound, CSC) through an intermediate degree (microstimulus, MS) to complete generalization (presence representation). This dimension also determines the temporal granularity with which predictions of the unconditioned stimulus (US) are learned.

P002116 further states that 'the degree of temporal generalization determines the temporal granularity with which US predictions are learned.' P002117 elaborates on the presence representation as one endpoint of the gradient. Together these passages anchor the definition as a conceptual dimension/property, not a representation or algorithm.

processed.entity: Stimulus representation (TD model of classical conditioning)
processed.definition: Stimulus representation in the TD model of classical conditioning is the way external conditioned and unconditioned stimuli are internally encoded as time-varying features for processing by the temporal-difference (TD) learning model. Specific instances such as the complete serial compound (CSC), microstimulus (MS), and presence representations differ in the degree of temporal generalization they impose among nearby time points, and the choice of representation strongly shapes the US prediction profiles and other predictions the TD model produces.

processed.definition: ISI-dependency is a core empirical property of classical conditioning describing how the associative strength between a conditioned stimulus (CS) and an unconditioned stimulus (US) varies as a function of the inter-stimulus interval (ISI) between their onsets: it is zero or slightly negative when the US onset is simultaneous with or earlier than the CS onset, rises to a maximum at a positive ISI, and then decays toward zero over an interval whose length depends on the response system. This ISI-curve shape is treated as a benchmark phenomenon that the TD model reproduces as one of its basic features.

supporting_observations.support: The passage directly describes the three-part shape of the ISI curve (zero/slightly negative at simultaneous or negative ISIs, peak at a positive ISI, decay to zero with response-system-dependent length) and explicitly identifies these as 'core properties of the TD model,' anchoring both the general pattern and the modeling context.

processed.definition: Facilitation of remote associations is a classical conditioning phenomenon in which the empty trace interval between a first conditioned stimulus (CS_A) and an unconditioned stimulus (US) is filled by a second CS (CS_B) to form a serial-compound stimulus, and the presence of CS_B increases both the rate and the asymptotic level of conditioning to the more temporally remote CS_A. The effect, experimentally demonstrated by Kehoe (1982), is also reproduced by temporal-difference (TD) models such as the TD model with a presence representation.

supporting_observations.support: Passage P002123 directly states that 'if the empty trace interval between a first CS (CSA) and the US is filled with a second CS (CSB) to form a serial-compound stimulus, then conditioning to CSA is facilitated' and that the TD model shows 'facilitation of both the rate of conditioning and the asymptotic level of conditioning of the first CS due to the presence of the second CS,' consistent with Kehoe (1982). P002124 continues the same discussion in the TD-model simulations subsection of Chapter 14.

processed.definition: It is a classical conditioning phenomenon originally demonstrated by Egger and Miller (1962), in which—using two overlapping conditioned stimuli (CSs) in a delay conditioning procedure—an earlier-onset CSA substantially reduces conditioning to a later-onset CSB, even though CSB has a closer temporal relationship with the unconditioned stimulus (US). It is frequently cited as a benchmark result that temporal-difference (TD) models reproduce via a bootstrapping mechanism, which standard Rescorla–Wagner-type models have difficulty explaining.

supporting_observations.support: P002124 names the Egger and Miller (1962) experiment with two overlapping CSs in a delay configuration and reports that 'the presence of CSA substantially reduced conditioning to CSB as compared to controls in which CSA was absent' despite CSB being in a better temporal relationship with the US; P002126 explains that the TD model accounts for the effect because 'an earlier predictive stimulus takes precedence over a later predictive stimulus' due to bootstrapping, and explicitly contrasts this capacity with Rescorla–Wagner-type models.

processed.definition: Temporal primacy overriding blocking is a classical conditioning phenomenon, originally a prediction of the temporal-difference (TD) model, in which the usual blocking effect is reversed when a newly-added second conditioned stimulus (CS) begins earlier in time than the pretrained blocking CS, so that the earlier CS gains associative strength and the pretrained CS loses it. It was confirmed experimentally by Kehoe, Schreurs, and Graham (1987) using the rabbit nictitating membrane preparation, and arises from the TD model's bootstrapping (backing-up) mechanism, which gives temporal precedence to the earlier predictive stimulus.

processed.definition: The rabbit nictitating membrane preparation is a well-established classical (Pavlovian) conditioning paradigm in rabbits in which extension of the nictitating membrane (third eyelid) serves as the conditioned response. processed.definition: Extinction in classical conditioning is the process by which a conditioned stimulus (CS) loses its predictive relationship to an unconditioned stimulus (US) when the US is no longer presented, causing the CS's associative strength to weaken and its ability to evoke a conditioned response or act as a conditioned reinforcer to diminish.

processed.definition: Complete Serial Compound (CSC) is a stimulus/input representation for the TD model in which a stimulus triggers a sequence of distinct short-duration internal signals—one per time step—continuing until the onset of the unconditioned stimulus, so that each post-stimulus time step is represented as a separate state. This temporal granularity makes the TD error state-dependent, causing the model's US prediction to rise exponentially across the CS–US interval and peak exactly at the US (reaching US intensity at asymptote), in contrast to simpler representations such as the presence representation that yield a near-constant prediction.

processed.definition: The microstimulus (MS) representation is a stimulus representation for the TD model of classical conditioning, introduced by Ludvig, Sutton, and Kehoe (2008), in which a compound stimulus is encoded as a set of microstimuli. processed.definition: The nictitating membrane response is a conditioned response (CR) in classical conditioning, most famously studied in rabbits, in which over conditioning trials the onset latency of the membrane's movement across the eye shortens while the amplitude of the anticipatory closure grows across the CS–US interval, reaching maximal closure near the expected time of the US. processed.definition: 行为主义心理学中关于学习与行为的一种理论观点，强调刺激与反应之间的直接联结，将学习视为无需价值函数或环境模型的、最简单的策略获取方式；该观点曾居主导地位，后被潜在学习等实验所挑战。

processed.definition: 心理学家，以潜在学习（latent learning）概念最为人所知；他在解释 Blodgett 等人的实验时提出，动物能在没有显在奖惩的情况下通过探索习得环境的"认知地图"，并在动机驱动下利用该地图规划目标导向的路径。

supporting_observations.support: P002167 明确将 Tolman 标识为心理学家，并将其与潜在学习概念紧密关联，记载了他用'认知地图'解释 Blodgett 等人实验的核心主张——动物可在无奖惩时习得环境地图并受动机驱动时使用它；P002168 进一步补充了他对认知地图习得机制的解释（通过 S–S 关联和期望理论），与当前定义中'通过探索习得认知地图'的表述一致。

processed.definition: Tolman 提出的心理学联想学习理论，认为动物在探索环境时通过经历连续刺激习得 S–S（刺激-刺激）联想并据此构建认知地图；在该理论下，当前刺激的出现会生成对下一刺激的期望，这一机制与控制工程中的系统辨识类似。

supporting_observations.support: 该观察直接来自 Sutton & Barto 第 14 章对 Tolman 期望理论的引述，明确给出三方面锚定：① 理论归属为 Tolman 对认知地图习得的解释；② 核心机制为通过经历连续刺激学习 S–S 联想；③ 给定当前刺激即生成对下一刺激的期望，并与控制工程中的系统辨识进行类比。

processed.definition: 刺激–刺激联想（S–S Associations）是 Tolman 提出的认知地图学习机制，指动物在探索环境中经历连续刺激时习得的前后刺激之间的预测性关联；它构成心理学期望理论的基础，在强化学习中类比于控制工程中的系统辨识，常以状态–后续状态（S–S'）配对作为监督学习的训练样本。

supporting_observations.support: 原文直接陈述 Tolman 以'动物在探索环境过程中经历连续刺激习得 S–S 联想'来解释认知地图的形成，并将 S–S 联想定位为期望理论（'given S–S associations, the occurrence of a stimulus generates an expectation about the stimulus to come next'）的基础；同时给出与系统辨识的类比以及 S–S' 训练样本形式，直接支撑定义中关于机制、理论基础、类比和训练样本的全部要点。

processed.entity: 行为主义/认知心理学之争
processed.definition: 心理学中长期存在的核心争论，指行为主义（强调可观察的刺激–反应关系）与认知心理学（强调内部表征与心智结构）之间的对立；潜在学习等实验结果被视作推动并持续支撑该争论的关键证据。

supporting_observations.support: 原文明确指出 Tolman 用潜在学习等结果解释动物具备'认知地图'，并直接表述为'Explanations of results like these led to the enduring controversy lying at the heart of the behaviorist/cognitive dichotomy in psychology'，为'行为主义 vs 认知心理学'的对立核心以及潜在学习作为关键证据两条要点提供了直接文本支持。

processed.definition: Habitual behavior is a mode of behavior in which stimulus-triggered action patterns are performed automatically under the control of antecedent stimuli rather than by evaluating expected outcomes, and it typically develops after extended repetition of goal-directed behavior. It is the psychological counterpart of model-free reinforcement learning and is distinguished from goal-directed behavior by its insensitivity to outcome devaluation.

supporting_observations.support: Provides the core definitional claims: stimulus-triggered, performed more-or-less automatically, controlled by antecedent stimuli, responds quickly to an accustomed environment but cannot quickly adjust to environmental changes.

Anchors the developmental claim (extended repetition turns goal-directed behavior into habitual behavior) and the outcome-devaluation criterion (overtrained rats' lever-pressing is insensitive to devaluation, evidence of habitual control).
States the model-free/model-based RL analogy and identifies outcome-devaluation experiments as the standard test for distinguishing habitual from goal-directed control.
Attributes the formal proposal of the habitual–goal-directed / model-free–model-based correspondence to Daw, Niv, and Dayan (2005), grounding the RL analogy historically.
Equates habitual with model-free behavior, links it to dorsolateral striatum processing, and notes dopamine signaling as a neural correlate, reinforcing the model-free identity.

processed.definition: Goal-directed behavior is purposeful behavior controlled by knowledge of the value of goals and the relationship between actions and their consequences, in contrast to habitual behavior that is triggered by antecedent stimuli and performed more-or-less automatically. It is said to be controlled by its consequences, corresponds to model-based reinforcement learning, and is empirically identified by sensitivity to outcome devaluation, giving it the advantage of flexibly adapting when the environment changes its response to the animal's actions.

supporting_observations.support: Directly anchors the core definition: goal-directed behavior is purposeful, controlled by knowledge of the value of goals and action–consequence relationships, is said to be controlled by its consequences, and can rapidly change behavior when the environment's reactions change.
Anchors the model-based RL correspondence and the standard empirical identification via outcome-devaluation experiments distinguishing it from habitual behavior.

Supports the outcome-devaluation sensitivity and flexibility characterization: the Adams (1982) experiment shows non-overtrained rats acted in a goal-directed manner sensitive to their knowledge of action outcomes, and that with enough repetition goal-directed behavior tends to turn into habitual behavior.
Supports the cross-domain mapping to model-based reinforcement learning and the distinction from habitual (model-free) behavior used throughout the source.
Confirms the model-based equivalence and the neural correlates (dorsomedial striatum, OFC) that researchers associate with goal-directed behavior, reinforcing the cross-domain identity.

processed.definition: A model-free policy in reinforcement learning that stores direct stimulus–response links (state-to-action mappings) in place of action values, so that decisions can be made without consulting an environment model. It is presented as analogous to habitual, stimulus–response behavior and is contrasted with both action-value methods and model-based strategies.

supporting_observations.support: The source text directly states that a cached policy is 'a different model-free strategy' that 'rely[s] on a cached policy instead of action values, making direct links from S1 to L and from S2 to R,' and that 'in neither of these strategies do decisions rely on an environment model,' anchoring every key claim in the definition (model-free nature, direct S→A links replacing action values, and no environment-model lookup).

processed.definition: An outcome-devaluation experiment is an experimental paradigm, originating in animal learning research, in which an animal (or human subject) is first trained to perform an action for a reward and then has the value of that outcome reduced—potentially to zero or a negative value—after which continued performance is measured to determine whether the behavior is habitual (insensitive to the change in outcome value) or under goal-directed control (sensitive to it). It provides the empirical bridge between the psychological distinction of habitual versus goal-directed behavior and the computational distinction between model-free and model-based reinforcement learning, and is widely used in neuroscience to localize the brain structures supporting each mode.

supporting_observations.support: Anchors the core definition: initial rewarded learning stage followed by changing the reward value (including to zero or negative) to test whether behavior is habitual or goal-directed; also documents the canonical Adams and Dickinson (1981) rat lever-press/sucrose/lithium-chloride procedure as a concrete instance.

Explicitly states that outcome-devaluation experiments provide information about whether behavior is habitual or under goal-directed control, and links them to the model-free/model-based RL distinction.

Shows the paradigm is reused as a behavioral readout in neuroscience by inactivating a brain area before the test stage, demonstrating that the paradigm itself is the devaluation-plus-performance test, not a brain-inactivation procedure.

Confirms the paradigm is used with both rodents (Yin & Knowlton, 2006) and human subjects via functional imaging (Valentin, Dickinson & O'Doherty, 2007), supporting the broadened scope of the definition.

Cites Dickinson (1980, 1985) and Donahoe and Burgos (2000) as key references discussing the paradigm and its interpretation, supporting the claim that it is a well-established paradigm with an interpretive literature.

processed.definition: Lithium chloride (LiCl) is an inorganic ionic compound formed from lithium and chlorine, appearing as a white, water-soluble crystalline salt with a wide range of industrial and laboratory uses (e.g., desiccant, brazing flux, chemical reagent). In behavioral and conditioning research, it is notably employed as a nausea-inducing agent that, when injected after an animal consumes a food, produces conditioned taste aversion and thereby lowers the reward value of that food in outcome-devaluation experiments.

supporting_observations.support: The observation's type label 'chemical agent' and the source passage (P002182) directly establish lithium chloride as a chemical used as a 'nausea-inducing poison' injected after non-contingent food consumption to devalue the food reward, and P002185 confirms its repeated use across sessions via 'lithium chloride injections' to decrease reward value—these facts anchor the second sentence of the definition.

processed.definition: Non-contingent food is food delivered to an animal independently of any particular behavior or action, rather than as a consequence of a specific response. It is typically used in experimental procedures—such as the outcome-devaluation paradigm—where it contrasts with contingent (behavior-dependent) food delivery to dissociate learned, response-outcome associations from mere sensory exposure to the food.

supporting_observations.support: Observation 3182 directly defines non-contingent food as pellets made available 'independently of their actions' (P002182), used as a stage in an outcome-devaluation paradigm. The source text describes the concrete procedure (15-minute free access in the training chamber with the lever retracted) and its purpose (establishing the pre-devaluation baseline of the food's reward value), which supports both the general meaning and the outcome-devaluation use case stated in the definition. The aliases 'non-contingent pellets' and 'free-access to the pellets' further anchor the behavioral-independence aspect.

processed.definition: Extinction training in instrumental conditioning is a training procedure in which the response manipulandum (e.g., a lever) remains available to the animal but is disconnected from the reward dispenser, so that the previously learned response no longer produces its accustomed outcome. It is used to probe whether a learned instrumental response persists when its reinforcing consequence is no longer delivered, for example to dissociate goal-directed from habitual control of behavior.

supporting_observations.support: Both passages come from the Adams and Dickinson (1981) re-description in Sutton & Barto's RL textbook, and explicitly define extinction training in the instrumental-conditioning sense as a session in which 'the response lever was back in place but disconnected from the pellet dispenser so that pressing it did not release pellets.' This directly anchors the core operational feature (manipulandum present, reward delivery broken) and the testing purpose (whether the response rate is reduced when the outcome no longer follows), which are the two key identifying aspects of the instrumental-conditioning extinction procedure.

processed.definition: A cognitive map is a psychological construct, originating in mid-20th-century animal learning theory (notably Tolman), referring to an internal representation of the environment that an animal can use to guide navigation, planning, and choice—especially when conditions change unexpectedly—often as an alternative or complement to simple state–action or stimulus–response associations.

supporting_observations.support: Directly characterizes cognitive maps as mid-20th-century psychological constructs that animals learn as alternatives or additions to state–action associations and use to guide behavior when the environment changes unexpectedly.
Attributes the concept to Tolman and links it to the use of internal models to navigate mazes and select actions, providing the historical attribution and the navigation/planning dimension.

Provides a concrete experimental instantiation (Adams & Dickinson) showing a cognitive map linking actions to their outcomes and outcomes to their reward values, illustrating the action–outcome–consequence structure the concept supports.
Index entry confirming cognitive maps are an established psychology/neuroscience concept (pp. 363–364) cross-referenced with reinforcement learning, consistent with the general definition.

processed.definition: In instrumental conditioning, overtraining is a training condition in which a behavior is practiced well beyond the number of trials required for its initial acquisition. It is experimentally used to promote habit formation: such extended training reduces the behavior's sensitivity to outcome devaluation, thereby shifting control from goal-directed to habitual behavior.

supporting_observations.support: The passage describes Adams' (1982) experiment comparing overtrained rats (100 rewarded lever-presses) with non-overtrained rats, showing that devaluation strongly decreased lever-pressing in the non-overtrained group but had little or even enhancing effect in the overtrained group, supporting the claim that extended training reduces sensitivity to outcome devaluation and converts goal-directed behavior into a habit.

processed.definition: A theoretical proposal by Daw, Niv, and Dayan (2005) suggesting that animals run model-free and model-based reinforcement learning processes in parallel, with each proposing an action and the action proposed by the process currently judged more trustworthy—via running measures of confidence—being selected for execution. This arbitration mechanism predicts a shift from goal-directed to habitual behavioral control as experience accumulates.

supporting_observations.support: Both passages directly describe the Daw, Niv, and Dayan (2005) proposal: parallel model-free and model-based processes each proposing an action, selection of the action from the more trustworthy process as determined by running confidence measures, and the resulting prediction of a shift from goal-directed to habitual control with accumulated experience.

processed.entity: Tree pruning (search tree pruning in planning)
processed.definition: A planning technique that removes unpromising branches from the search tree to keep planning computationally tractable; in the model-based versus model-free discussion of reinforcement learning, it is noted as a source of mistakes that can make a model-free process appear more trustworthy than planning as experience accumulates.

supporting_observations.support: The passage directly defines tree-pruning as 'the removal of unpromising search tree branches' used 'to make planning feasible,' and immediately links it to the prediction that goal-directed (model-based) behavior will give way to habitual (model-free) behavior 'as more experience accumulates,' which grounds both the core technique and the contextual role in the definition.

processed.definition: Stimulus traces are mechanisms proposed in early theories of animal learning to address the problem of delayed reinforcement, and are considered antecedents to—and similar to—eligibility traces in reinforcement learning.

supporting_observations.support: The passage directly states that 'Eligibility traces are similar to stimulus traces of early theories' and frames both stimulus traces and value functions as 'mechanisms for addressing the problem of delayed reinforcement' that 'have antecedents in theories of animal learning,' anchoring the definition's claims about their origin in animal learning theory, their function, and their relationship to eligibility traces.

processed.definition: Multi-agent reinforcement learning is a subfield of reinforcement learning concerned with how populations of agents learn through interaction, often under a shared or common reward signal, which gives rise to structural credit assignment problems and settings such as cooperative games and team problems. It connects to the social aspects of behavior, the study of agent behavior in complex ecologies, and computational neuroscience, and is surveyed in the broader literature by works such as Nowé, Vrancx, and De Hauwere (2012).

supporting_observations.support: Anchors the entity as a subfield of reinforcement learning and explicitly links it to social aspects of behavior and to agent behavior in complex ecologies.

Defines the field as concerning learning by populations of reinforcement learning agents, introduces the cooperative game / team problem setting with a common reward signal, and names the structural credit assignment problem that arises among team members.
Confirms the 'wider field' framing of multi-agent reinforcement learning and supports the cited survey (Nowé, Vrancx, and De Hauwere, 2012) as part of the entity's identity.

processed.entity: Klopf's drive-reinforcement theory of classical conditioning
processed.definition: Klopf (1988) 提出的经典条件作用理论，属于对时序差分（TD）模型的扩展，用以解释更多实验现象，例如习得曲线呈 S 形的特征。

processed.definition: 在延迟强化学习情境下，用于解释长时间延迟（如味觉厌恶条件作用中长达数小时）下学习如何发生的一类理论，其核心立场是与衰减痕迹理论相对立，认为延迟学习不能仅靠记忆痕迹的自然衰减来解释，而需要借助记忆间的干扰等机制。

supporting_observations.support: 原文明确指出味觉厌恶条件作用中'长达数小时的延迟'催生了 interference theories，并将其定位为 decaying-trace theories 的'替代方案'（alternatives），同时该段落位于第14章心理学部分且与 delayed reinforcement 直接关联，锚定了该术语的义项边界——它是延迟强化学习背景下、相对于衰减痕迹理论的替代性理论解释。

processed.definition: A class of learning theories that explain delayed reinforcement by assuming that the trace left by a conditioning stimulus decays over time. It is typically contrasted with interference theories as one of two main candidate explanations for long-delay learning phenomena such as taste aversion conditioning.

supporting_observations.support: The source passage directly states that 'interference theories [arose] as alternatives to decaying-trace theories', anchoring both the core decaying-trace mechanism and the rivalry with interference theories for explaining long-delay learning; the model_quote preserves the exact phrasing about the two competing frameworks.

processed.entity: Gopnik et al. (2004) Bayesian theory of children's causal model learning
processed.definition: Gopnik、Glymour、Sobel、Schulz、Kushnir 和 Danks（2004）提出的贝叶斯理论，旨在以贝叶斯推理框架解释儿童如何学习因果模型。它以因果图（causal maps）和贝叶斯网络（Bayes nets）等结构化表征作为核心工具，关注儿童的因果推理与模型建构。

processed.definition: Taste-aversion conditioning is a paradigm in classical conditioning distinguished by an unusually long delay—up to several hours—between a taste stimulus and its associated negative consequence. This long delay posed a challenge to decaying-trace theories of learning and led researchers to propose interference theories as alternative explanations.

supporting_observations.support: 原文明确定义该范式属于经典条件作用，并指出其延迟可达数小时，以及该延迟促使研究者用干扰理论替代衰减痕迹理论；这些是当前义项的核心特征。

processed.definition: Reward, in animal learning psychology, is a stimulus (an object or event) that an animal will approach and work for, functioning to increase the likelihood of a preceding behavior. It is conceptually distinct from the formal reinforcement-learning reward signal (a scalar number) and encompasses both primary rewards (produced by evolutionarily built-in neural responses such as food taste or successful escape) and higher-order rewards (stimuli that directly or indirectly predict primary reward).

supporting_observations.support: The passage directly defines reward as an object or event an animal will approach and work for, contrasts it with the RL scalar signal Rt, and describes subtypes (primary, higher-order, secondary), all of which ground the current psychological-entity reading.

processed.definition: In animal learning psychology, a penalty is an object or event that the animal typically avoids and is delivered as a consequence of 'bad' behavior in order to change that behavior. It functions as the aversive counterpart to reward, used to reduce undesired behavior rather than to reinforce desired responses.

supporting_observations.support: Provides the direct textbook definition of penalty as an object or event the animal usually avoids, given as a consequence of 'bad' behavior to change it; also establishes penalty as the aversive counterpart to reward in the animal learning psychology context.

processed.definition: 强化信号（reinforcement signal）是强化学习中在任意时刻取正、负或零的标量信号，其功能是驱动学习算法对智能体的策略、价值估计或环境模型进行更新，因此与单纯标示行为好坏的奖励信号有明确区分。在大多数算法中它以TD误差等形式由奖励分量（初级强化）与价值预测差（条件性强化）共同构成，其神经对应物被假设为多巴胺神经元的相位活动。
